items.body: Spanish, Berlin-based Irene Aranda is primarily a classically trained pianist and self-taught in free jazz and free improvisation hyper-pianist who employs the piano as a sonic environment, using preparations and extended techniques to uncover enigmatic textures and resonances. Irene Aranda - MAY (Relative Pitch, 2026) MAY features Aranda in a trio with Spanish sax player Don Malfon (aka Alfonso Muñoz) and Japanese-born vocal (and visual) artist Ami Yamasaki in a studio recording from Berlin in January 2026. The eight free improvised pieces are titled as wishes that begin with “May the games begin”, go through “May you have many more meaning in Urdu”, and end with “May you all hate free jazz” (apparently, with the most free jazz playing by Aranda here). This unconventional trio take their respective singular sonic palettes of Malfon, Aranda, and Yamasaki to the extreme, obviously, with an array of highly personal extended techniques - breathing (with mutes and objects, in the case of Malfon), echolocation vocals (Yamasaki), and playing (or pounding) inside the piano (Aranda). Each piece visits a distinct, intense, and deeply visceral, immersive territory, shaped by radical, urgent, and Dadaist approaches to breath, space, vibration, or sound at all, often on the verge of chaos. The trio keeps searching for friction and compatibility of its strong-minded musical personalities. Occasionally, the trio’s dark humour and Yamasaki’s sensual, lyrical, and often pixie-like (wordless) voice introduce a more accessible vein into the uncompromising sonic collisions. There is no end to the inventive, inimitable dynamics of this trio or to its unpredictable, captivating lexicon. Prepare for the most physical, wildest possible ride yet a highly rewarding one where even the most discerning listeners may find themselves caught off guard. MAY by Irene Aranda The Dark Deniers - Tales of Freedom (Self-Released, 2026) Aranda leaves the piano aside and is the mastermind, conductor, vocalist and bandleader of The Dark Deniers ensemble, a Berlin-based experimental octet featuring trumpeters Germán García and Brad Henkel, alto sax player Grgur Savić, baritone sax player Pablo Muñoz, trombonist Gerhard Gschlößl, guitarist Christian Kühn, and drummer Martial Frenzel. The Dark Deniers mix dramatic poetic texts (of John Masefield, Maya Angelou, John Donne, Lord Byron, Antonio Machado, Alfonsina Storni, Anne Bradstreet, Paul Éluard, Gilbert Chesterton, and Dylan Thomas), focusing on mortality, resistance, existential collapse, time, and transformation, with Butch Morris’ conduction principle, free jazz, avant-rock, metal, and free improvisation. The Dark Deniers’ debut album, Tales of Freedom , was recorded live at Studio Zentri Fuge in Berlin in May 2026. Aranda is a capable, evocative and passionate vocalist and a commanding leader who leads this organism-like, powerful ensemble through ten pieces, beginning with the ritualist, pagan-like prayer (or provocation): “We are The Dark Deniers. Let us summon Death from a summer woman”, and soon lets this poetic phrase bloom into a funky storm. This ensemble sounds as if it searches for a primordial, pre-cosmic state of raw sound, as expressed in the aptly titled “Vocifera”, with Aranda’s effective growling vocals. Throughout Tales of Freedom , Aranda uses the poetic texts, the language (the English, Spanish, and French ones), and the ensemble’s complex sonic palettes as material she can shape, mould, and invent anew as impossible yet intricate, organic structures, with a touching, thought-provoking, and often subversive pathos. The Dark Deniers, like the trio with Malfon and Yamasaki, also embrace chaos, but in a different approach. Aranda shapes the sonic architectures and literary texts from chaos and sheer visceral freedom, and vice versa, always flirting joyfully with fiery, explosive dynamics, danger and risk-taking, or as Aranda puts it: “play with death the way that children play with fire”. Any round with Aranda’s music is bound to take listeners on the most unpredictable yet deeply immersive wild ride, inspire and equip us all with enough invigorating food for resisting thoughts, until, one day, Aranda and The Dark Deniers will rule the world. items._cn_summary: 本乐评聚焦西班牙钢琴家Irene Aranda的两张作品，均以激进即兴为核心。三重奏专辑《MAY》收录八首自由即兴作品，曲目以"May"开头的祈愿句命名，从游戏开始到对自由爵士的反讽，Aranda与萨克斯手Don Malfon、声乐艺术家Ami Yamasaki在柏林录音中各自调用扩展技法——钢琴内弦击打、呼吸与物体塞入萨克斯、回声定位唱法——碰撞出高度身体性、近乎混沌的声响场域，偶尔以荒诞幽默与精灵般的无词人声提供短暂的可入路径。《Tales of Freedom》则由Aranda率柏林八人实验乐团The Dark Deniers，融合Butch Morris指挥法、自由爵士、前卫摇滚、金属与即兴，文本选自Masefield、Angelou、Donne等十位诗人的诗作，围绕死亡、抗拒、时间与蜕变展开。Relative Pitch属专注自由即兴的小厂牌，乐评描述详尽，兼具创作方法与听觉效果分析。

items.body: In 1998, a remarkable album was released as a collaborative exchange between Sonar and Muslimgauze. Eric van Wonterghem and Dirk Ivens (Sonar) created four remixes of tracks by Bryn Jones (Muslimgauze), and the process was reciprocated. However, what wasn’t known at the time was that Bryn Jones had actually produced a total of 16 remixes, leaving it up to Eric and Dirk to decide what to do with them. Following the release, performances featuring both projects were even planned, but tragedy struck when Bryn Jones passed away in early 1999. The British project Muslimgauze was extraordinary—a project I deeply admired for its sound and its unique blend of Tribal and Middle Eastern influences. Now, so many years later, these Belgian legends have decided to release the original remixes Muslimgauze created for Sonar as a standalone album, undoubtedly driven by deep respect and admiration for Bryn Jones’s masterful body of work. The result is surprising, presenting a completely transformed Sonar sound that fits seamlessly into the Muslimgauze universe. The Belgians’ signature Power-Noise is absorbed by the force of Tribal rhythms and an Eastern atmosphere, characterized by the authentic sounds of traditional instruments. Layered on top are samples of plaintive chants and voices that further enhance the mood. Muslimgauze didn’t merely create remixes; Jones undertook a complete reconstruction of the Sonar material. The overall sound is highly minimalist and perfectly embodies the Muslimgauze aesthetic. I am also struck by the brilliant stereo effects emanating from the speakers, which lend an extra touch of distinction to the production. Through this album, Muslimgauze sounds as if the project is still alive—or perhaps newly reborn. As far as I’m concerned, this is a wonderful experience. (Rating:8). Listen to “Outtake 3”: Outtake 3 by Sonar vs Muslimgauze About Sonar Sonar is the Belgian industrial and techno side-project of Dirk Ivens, also known for his work in Klinik and Dive. The project began with Ivens working alongside Patrick Stevens (Hypnoskull); Eric Van Wonterghem (Insekt, Monolith) later joined as the group’s other core member. Sonar released its self-titled debut album in 1996, followed by “Dislocated” and “On Mission Inside” in 1997. In 1998, Sonar exchanged remixes with British artist Muslimgauze (Bryn Jones, 17 June 1961 – 14 January 1999) for the collaborative album “Sonar vs Muslimgauze”, released via Prodam Records. Jones died in January 1999, shortly after the exchange was completed. “Outtakes” gathers the remaining Muslimgauze-made remixes of Sonar material that were left unused at the time.
items._genre: industrial / tribal / dark ambient / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是比利时工业电子团体 Sonar 与英国穆斯林团体 Muslimgauze 之间一次未完成的合作遗作的正式发布。1998年双方交换混音时，Bryn Jones 为 Sonar 的素材制作了16首混音，最终只有4首被采用。其余混音沉寂多年后由 Sonar 成员决定公开。Jones 的处理方式远非简单的混音，而是对原始材料进行了彻底的解构与重建：Sonar 标志性的力量噪音质感被部落节奏与中东氛围吞噬，传统乐器采样与哀婉的人声碎片叠加其上，形成极简主义的听觉景观。立体声效果的设计为整体增添了空间感与纵深感。原始合作背景与创作者的意外离世赋予这张专辑某种纪念碑式的意义，其将工业结构与民族声响的融合做到了高度统一。

items.body: For the dedicated fans of wind player, composer, and teacher Julius Hemphill, the last two years are shaping up to be an extraordinary era of listening and tribute. Hemphill passed away in 1995 and though he never fell away from the community’s eye, we seem, currently, to be paying much more attention. For a good bit of that,it seems we have Marty Ehrlich to thank. Ehrlich worked with Hemphill and his music over the decades, showing that connection clearly in his own body of work. In 2022 New World released The Boyé Multi-National Crusade For Harmony ( reviewed here ), a 7 disc set of unreleased archival Hemphill recordings, curated by Ehrlich. Now we are presented with Open Air: The Complete Saxophone Quartet Compositions of Julius Hemphill . We don’t need to ask which quartet we’re talking about. Hemphill’s work (along with Oliver Lake, David Murray, and Hamiet Bluett) as a co-founder of the World Saxophone Quartet did not create the sax quartet, but did so much to map its possibilities and implications that it’s hard to imagine how the sax quartet got along before their work. But there’s more. Two thirds of the music Hemphill wrote for sax quartet was recorded by the WSQ, but one third of the music here (14 or so tracks) was discovered in Hemphill’s papers after his death. Ehrlich discovered these while doing archive work with Hemphill’s publisher. It’s somewhat amazing to encounter, 30 years after Hemphill’s death, 14 new pieces for saxophone quartet. It’s like suddenly discovering 14 new Goldberg Variations. (And, no, I do not agree that this is an overwrought analogy. Here’s a bias check for you: there are times when I’m listening to Hemphill’s quartets and I’m completely taken over. In the reverie or ecstasy or elation of those moments, I have been known to think things like, “When God said, let there be music, this is exactly what he was talking about!” I’m not saying I can argue a rational basis for that view, just that sometimes you can look to your elation for a truer kind of truth.) Ehrlich forms a clutch of saxophonists—Allan Chase, Rob Debellis, Brian Landrus, Andy Laster, Jeff Lederer, Lisa Parrott, and Jason Robinson—into a few quartets, recording the whole body of work over a number of months in 2025. The listening is exactly as one would hope. With faithful, passionate, and fascinated renditions of the tunes by musicians who love them, and infused with improvisation that leads to revelation. For example, the WSQ piece, “Revue,” is perhaps the best known sax quartet piece out there, and listening, I can’t help but expect the solo from the WSQ’s second album to come after the statement of the head. It’s a dumb expectation, of course, but Brian Landrus’s solo takes me by surprise and winds along a path that returns to the tune by a way I’ve never been before. The harmonies and ensemble playing of this choir of sax angels can be heart stopping, but the solo on top of those are just as amazing. Ehrlich has shown—particularly on The Hard Blues by his Julius Hemphill Sextet—that he can render the master’s work with skill and authenticity. It’s important because this music is not just interesting and brilliant. It is hard, bluesy, and culturally real as anything you can imagine. It is exactly this mixture of “Stax funk and ‘out’ sensibilities” (to use Tim Berne’s phrase), mixed with an intellectual playfulness, that made Hemphill the composer that he was and keeps me obsessed with his oeuvre thirty years after he’s gone. In case I have to say it, 5 stars. OPEN AIR: The Complete Saxophone Quartet Compositions of Julius Hemphill by Marty Ehrlich Other release... Circle the Heart - Marty Ehrlich and Julius Hemphill (Relative Pitch, 2026) Circle the Heart also explores the saxophone choir space (a duo is a subset of a choir, right?) and gives us insight into the musical collaboration of Hemphill and Ehrlich. The set is a discovered recording of a glorious 1982 concert. Of six tunes, all are Ehrlich compositions save the last, and, in an odd way, this seems only to confirm the shared DNA between the two. Besides, the intrigue is in the improv. The two are so in tune with each other that it’s not enough to call their duo a conversation, so much as a telepathic bonding. Again, I may be over-egging the metaphor, but it really is that good. Circle the Heart by Marty Ehrlich, Julius Hemphill Dogon A.D. - Julius Hemphill (New World Records) Dogon A.D. may be the most cited gateway drug to outmusic of any record out there. The 1972 masterpiece—with its title track in an insanely addictive 11—was re-released in 2011 by International Phonograph. FJB reviewed it here , giving it five stars and listing it as one of the top 20 free jazz recs of all time. That New World is re-releasing it—remastered and co-produced by the ubiquitous Ehrlich—is only good news. I just thought I’d bring it to your attention. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了Julius Hemphill为萨克斯四重奏创作的全部作品，由长期合作者Marty Ehrlich策划并组织多位萨克斯手录制完成。其中约三分之一的曲目是Hemphill去世后在其遗留手稿中新发现的14首作品，此前从未被演奏或录制。Ehrlich将七位萨克斯手编组为多个四重奏，历时数月完成全部录音。评论指出，这些演绎充满忠实与热情，编曲的和声与合奏层次极具感染力，而独奏段落同样展现出令人意外的即兴走向——例如Brian Landrus在经典曲目《Revue》中的独奏开辟了全新的回归路径。整张专辑既是对Hemphill音乐遗产的完整梳理，也为萨克斯四重奏这一编制提供了新的曲目资源与演绎范本。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张9CD合辑梳理了作曲家兼即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim四十年的录音生涯。1980年她离开韩国赴美，从传统韩国音乐训练转向电子音乐与作曲，师从Lou Harrison与Terry Riley。作品核心在于对古乐器玄琴（komungo，公元四世纪以来的五尺长琴）的革命性扩展，通过计算机接口与信号处理将这件以冥想、空寂、缓慢为特质的乐器推入当代即兴语境。她以有限音色的传统乐器与世界级大师如Derek Bailey、Kronos Quartet、Gerry Hemingway、Tony Oxley、Bill Frisell等同台。合辑五张光盘收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张记录即兴合作，涵盖图形谱创作、用西方乐器转译韩国音乐的早期实验。每件作品都扎根韩国传统，但呈现出截然不同的面貌，印证了她赴美开拓新音乐的初衷。

items.body: roshambo (trio) Just when you thought there was nothing left to be done with the ‘sound-silence-sound’ strain of composition that can be heard almost ubiquitously in certain experimental music circles of late, here comes diatribes and Cristián Alvear with another excellent and fresh-sounding example of the genre. The composite sounds framed by silence are as gorgeous and ear-catching as ever, but each member of the trio adds something new and unexpected to the mix. If you think you’ve heard the name of the piece somewhere before, you’re probably thinking of the version on diatribes’ album “A new castle”; this new trio version was recorded in Santiago, Chile during the Swiss duo’s recent South American tour. You may also be thinking that the delicately plucked acoustic guitar strings heard from Alvear on recordings of compositions such as Radu Malfatti’s ‘shizuka ni furu ame’ and Ryoko Akama’s ‘Hermit’ would complement the various rumbles, hisses, and tones heard on the original version of ‘roshambo’ rather nicely. You may well be right, but Alvear chooses a different path on this occasion, contributing a number of e-bow hums, body knocks, and string scrapes to the proceedings — not a clearly plucked string to be heard. Cyril Bondi is in a much more rhythmic mood this time round, his acoustic objects gently tapping, ticking, brushing, rattling and shaking through the various figures. His partner-in-art d’incise, as well as reprising various electronic tones, also contributes a number of field recordings that vary from clearly recognisable as such to ambiguous in origin. I think this is the first time I’ve heard field recordings used in this sort of composition, and it’s very effective. Make a sound together, pause; make another sound together, pause; repeat for twenty minutes or so. It sounds like such a simple recipe, but the results are far from dull or unimaginative. Maybe it’s due to the use of field recordings, but to me this version of ‘roshambo’ seems more reminiscent than any other work I’ve heard in this style of a series of snapshots or polaroids in a slideshow, the continuous cycling through from one image to the next. The sounds share photographs’ ambiguous location somewhere between discrete objects and moments in a stream or narrative, repeating a regular form while constantly varying timbre and harmony. Through its variations on a theme or permutations of an idea, “roshambo (trio)” offers a critique of time and duration through an absorbing, open-ended musical experiment, at once sculptural and ephemeral.     diatribes Cristián Alvear 1000füssler
items._genre: experimental / sound-silence composition / e-bow / field recording / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张作品延续"声音—静默—声音"的创作传统，但通过三位音乐家的不同手法赋予全新面貌。瑞士二人组diatribes与智利吉他手Cristián Alvear合作的三重奏版本在圣地亚哥录制完成，区别于二人组专辑中的原始版本。Alvear放弃了以往作品中的清晰拨弦，转而使用e-bow嗡鸣、敲击琴体与刮擦琴弦；Bondi以多种节奏性物件（敲击、摩擦、震动）铺陈；d'incise则在电子音色之外引入田野录音，从清晰可辨到来源模糊，扩展了此类作品的声响边界。整张作品持续约二十分钟，以简单的"共同发声—停顿"结构循环往复，却在音色与和声上不断变化，如同一组幻灯片式的快照，既批判性地审视时间与持续性，又呈现雕塑般坚实又转瞬即逝的听觉实验。

items.body: Friendship Survival Guide arrives as a blessing and a gift. In many ways we are still mourning the loss of Jóhann Jóhannsson, as his music is woven into the fabric of our lives. In the eight ensuing years, a few posthumous recordings have been released, along with a pair of box sets collecting his oeuvre; but the composer’s voice has been mostly silent since then. Enter close friend Adam Wiltzie, who earlier had collaborated with Jóhannsson on the scores for The Theory of Everything and Arrival. Wiltzie had held onto the analog tape loops from these sessions and later recorded guitars under the guidance of Steve Albini before Albini’s own passing, adding an extra layer of urgent melancholy. Friendship Survival Guide is an elegiac statement, approved by Jóhannsson’s family, that is not as much about surviving a friendship as it is about the experience of losing a friend. Wiltzie honors Jóhannsson while extending his legacy, completing an “artifact they created together” and offering it to the world in hopes that the healing might continue. As one might expect from the co-founder of Stars of the Lid, the music is as much ambient as modern composition, a melding of disciplines that forms a harmonious whole. The poignant “September Nineteen Sixty Nine” leads off the set; in this month, both composers were born but two days apart. The opening notes are like a lift-off, the launching of a life; in this case, two lives that would eventually intertwine. Immediately one is impressed by the brass and strings, the stately drama, the grand chords, surging first to one peak and then another. In less than three minutes, Wiltzie encapsulates all of his friend’s astonishing talents. The two-part “Dazed and Reflective Glory” introduces an abrasion of notes, like fading memories, corroded tapes, sheet music nibbled by moths. This abrasion fades in the second half as clearer, more insistent notes shine through, as if to suggest that time will not decorate this memory with rust. Every time the notes fade, we fear it will be the last, but we have learned otherwise. When the gentle choir begins to sing on “Mourners Will Be Outcast,” one thinks less of a funeral service than of an ascension, with new compositions wafting through the ether, descending through the clouds, borne on the mist and dew. Even as the choir recedes, the organ continues to play. Forboding clouds gather in “Exceptional Proportions,” threatening a deluge that thankfully does not occur. Instead there lies tenderness and hope in the nourishing rain of “Give Into Gravity.” The piece is an invitation to incorporate grief with its worthy companion, gratitude, and never to allow the first to walk alone. The choir returns like the acknowledgment of a prayer. The first single, “White Gloves & Turtlenecks,” is also the album’s shortest piece; and contains the album’s most overt violin melody, like a voice cutting through the fog. The track is matched with a video: the first part of a continuing story, promising more. In contrast, “Soft Favourites” is by far the album’s longest and most ambient piece, a soft reflection like a walk home from the chapel in slowly-falling snow. Midway through the piece, new chords emerge like visitations. The stars are twinkling, sending messages of their own. The title “In Ever Decreasing Circles” suggests fate closing in, the inevitable weight of time. Echo and breath populate the composition, along with some surprising glissandos that recall the score for Arrival. Yet this is only fitting, as a fine line exists between science and science fiction, just as there does between faith and fact. “Where You Are Now, Voyager” offers a clever play on words, referring not only to Voyager and its famed golden disc, but to the notes of a beloved composer, echoing through time; and to Jóhannsson himself, a voyager lost to us physically, but spiritually present, made all the more real through this exquisite resurrection of sound. (Richard Allen) Available here
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Adam Wiltzie为纪念已故挚友Jóhann Jóhannsson而完成的遗作。Wiltzie保留了两人早年合作《万物理论》与《降临》时的模拟磁带循环，并在Steve Albini的指导下录制吉他声部，使整张作品笼罩在一层紧迫的忧郁之中。专辑将氛围音乐与现代古典作曲融为一体，开篇曲以铜管与弦乐铺陈庄严的戏剧性张力，后续曲目则在模糊的记忆碎片与清晰的主题动机之间反复切换。合唱段落如同祈愿的回应，管风琴延续着哀悼与升天般的仪式感。专辑获得Jóhannsson家属认可，既是对逝者的悼念，也是对其遗产的延伸——通过完成两人共同创造的'艺术品'，Wiltzie试图让治愈的过程延续下去。

items.album: walakos ~ baseline distortion
items.excerpt: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. Much of the production is remarkably lucid, leaving enough space around the low end and harder electronic textures for small changes in timbre and rhythm to register. “Sapphire” establishes this physical vocabulary, while “Link State” opens it out, playing with depth and distance. “Recursion Error” is more nervous and insistent, its recurring rhythmic figures subtly displaced and reshaped as the trac
items.body: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. Much of the production is remarkably lucid, leaving enough space around the low end and harder electronic textures for small changes in timbre and rhythm to register. “Sapphire” establishes this physical vocabulary, while “Link State” opens it out, playing with depth and distance. “Recursion Error” is more nervous and insistent, its recurring rhythmic figures subtly displaced and reshaped as the track progresses. The collaborations broaden that vocabulary. “Ray” features guitar from Maksym Borovik (Maxy Force), whose pink Jazzcaster, in walakos’s own words, fills the space in the arrangement. It also gives the track a looser rhythmic character, with syncopated layers producing an elastic, slightly off-centre groove. “-RWD” reaches further into walakos’s personal history. It incorporates samples from earlier jams with his friend Mykyta Troiepольskyi (mutedbirds), a previous collaborator on “Wyciczone ptaki” from Interrupted. Old sounds resurface within a hazier, more melancholic piece, driven by a digitally treated voice that slips in and out of the surrounding texture. “1,74B COP” brings a very different voice into the album. A Colombian mother asking for news about her son serving in the Ukrainian military cuts through the electronic patterns. This creates a distancing effect giving the track an unexpected documentary weight. It is also a reminder that walakos is one half of warнякання with Anton Slepakov, a project that has produced one of the most effective ongoing chronicles of the full-scale invasion. What began as an attempt to register the war from the perspective of civilians living through it has inevitably changed as both Slepakov and walakos have since joined the Ukrainian military, shifting the project’s vantage point from life under invasion to the experience of those now serving within the war itself. The closing “Pixel (im)perfect” gathers clicks, pulses and synthetic fragments into a buoyant groove, punctuated by brief vocals and the return of the digitally treated voice heard earlier in the album. It makes for a fitting ending: busy, playful and still moving forward. Even when the music becomes melancholic or emotionally charged, baseline distortion keeps searching for movement. There is a tone of vintage in its sound but without the nostalgia. Rhythms change shape, layers thin out pulling details into focus and new variations flourish. The album is released by Dnipropop, a label that continues to function as a focal point for the city’s scene and artists orbiting beyond it. Walakos’s own note accompanying the album perhaps provides the more important context: he thanks the Ukrainian music community for continuing to make music, support one another and keep the ecosystem alive “despite all the circumstances”, dedicating his respect to those defending the country and remembering those still serving. photo by Roksolana Deineha To help us breakdown the production process of baseline distortion, I approached walakos directly. We have been in direct contact since I first interviewed him for the Ukrainian Field Notes series and it is always a pleasure and a privilige to get to speak to him. The liner notes describe baseline distortion as music written after “the familiar conditions of life had already changed”, with the title referring to a change in the basic frameworks through which you perceive the world. Musically, though, the album is very precise and rhythmically grounded, often establishing a stable groove and then altering what happens around it. What does “baseline distortion” mean to you, and did that idea influence the way you approached rhythm and structure on the record? “Baseline distortion” is a scientific term describing when an instrument’s readings begin to deviate from the norm under the influence of stimuli that are atypical for the sensor. Yes, our baseline settings have changed as well. It’s not just me, but I very often draw on my personal experience to interpret it through music. At first, one might think of constant stress, sleep deprivation, anxiety, and PTSD. But you say the tracks have become clearer and more balanced. And that, too, is baseline distortion. We all wanted a freer, more relaxed, and easier life. But times don’t let us choose. They dictate their own terms. And just like the approach to creating tracks—that’s exactly how the life of a civilian, who was supposed to become a soldier, ultimately transforms. More discipline, more clarity, more obedience. In music, this manifests in crisp grooves and adherence to a specific style. Before, I could afford to “blur” my musical vision and approach to production, but now I can’t. And I think this is an honest interpretation of my storytelling. Compared with Interrupted, there is a stronger pull towards UK club music here, but you rarely settle into a straightforward genre vocabulary. “Sapphire”, “Link State” and “Recursion Error” maintain recognisable rhythmic grids while constantly shifting accents and textures, while “Ray”, with Maksym Borovyk on guitar, opens up a much more spacious harmonic field. What drew you towards this UK-influenced rhythmic language, and how did the collaborations with Borovyk and Mykyta Troepolsky affect the direction of the album? Here, the general concept is followed. A soldier has a sphere of obedience, a sphere for interpreting orders, and personal aspects that you won’t lose no matter what. All of this is reflected in the music: there’s the “order” of the style, your interpretation of the “assigned task,” and the personal elements that keep you grounded in all of this and remain constant. Accordingly, the UK dictates the style (yes, I genuinely love and submit to it), and there’s room for interpretation through textures and accents. But all of that is just the “frame,” and there has to be a precious gem that you set into it: whether it’s a sample from a jam session with a friend that’s dear to your heart, or a melodic ambient guitar track with a shimmer from a buddy with whom you’re always joking around and almost never have a heart-to-heart. And that’s his very sincere voice. In “1,74B COP”, we suddenly hear the voice of a Colombian woman saying in Spanish that she is worried, wants to speak to her son and hasn’t heard from him for some time. Given that Colombians have travelled to fight on both the Ukrainian and Russian sides of the war, the recording introduces a disturbing ambiguity into the track. Where did you find it, who is the woman trying to contact, and what made you place this particular voice in “1,74B COP”? This is the most heart-wrenching part of the release. I’ve previously worked with this particular group of soldiers in the Ukrainian army. I have the utmost respect for these men. I’ve had deep conversations with some of them and continue to stay in touch even after they’ve been wounded or returned home. I was struck by these experienced men who led orderly, comfortable lives, who flew halfway across the globe because they couldn’t stand by and watch the injustice unfolding here. They shared my contact information with their loved ones, describing me as someone they could trust. Sometimes the mothers and wives of soldiers would call me, often in the middle of the night (since we’re in different time zones), asking about their well-being, even after I had already left my previous unit. As an empathetic person, I keenly felt the full range of emotions and struggles of a mother who, for a variety of reasons, couldn’t speak with her son. This voice is a symbolic representation of all the mothers waiting for their sons. I salute all the foreign soldiers who are helping us defend our land. As for the sample: I feel it would be unethical to use a recording of a private conversation, but I was able to convey the general meaning using modern synthesis. painting by Roksolana Deineha The album artwork depicts the painting Lost by Roksolana Deineha. What made you go for that image in particular? The painting is framed and hanging in our home. It has a very specific mood: danger, alertness, confusion, determination. I thought about the cover for quite a while; I even briefly considered going with the aesthetic of scientific instruments and their distortions. In the midst of this agonizing decision, we were talking with Roksolana — she asked me point-blank, “Describe what your album is about.” I described the moods and themes that guided me. Then she said, “Look at the wall. It seems like the guy in the painting knows what you’re talking about.” That’s when I stopped looking for another visual. You are currently serving in the Ukrainian military, while warнякання, your ongoing project with Anton Slepakov, confronts the experience of war much more explicitly through Anton’s words and your electronic compositions. baseline distortion comes out of the same changed reality but largely avoids verbal narrative. How has serving in the military affected your ability and desire to make music, and do walakos and warнякання now provide you with different ways of processing what you are living through? To be honest, war offers the living one gift amid the overwhelming horror, death, and destruction. A keener sense of life itself. Enjoying a cup of coffee, hugging a loved one, or passionately doing what you love. How does living under conditions of highly probable death affect me? In the same way. I want to drink in this life in big gulps: to greet the dawn, to see my parents, to drink coffee with friends, to create music… And yes… In warнякання, Anton’s voice truly sets the overall tone, and from that, I build music that serves as a framework and support for the stories Anton unfolds. This duo allows us to view our shared present through Anton’s eyes and highlight it. In my own project, there’s only my life, my stories, and my storytelling which shapes and determines the artistic expression of the tracks. There are plenty of stories in my life, which means there’s plenty of color for the musical canvas. I conceptualize the chosen stories, select the “musical colors,” and write the composition. That’s why even under similar circumstances the musical interpretation differs slightly. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以电子制作与声响实验为核心，标题中的"失真"并非主导元素，整体呈现出透明而清醒的质感，为低频与硬质电子纹理留出充分空间，使音色与节奏的细微变化得以凸显。吉他合作带来松弛的律动层次，切分音叠加形成弹性偏移的律动结构。专辑中嵌入了乌克兰战争的真实声音素材——一位哥伦比亚母亲询问在乌军中服役儿子的消息被置入电子肌理之中，形成了纪录片式的沉重感，将实验电子与战争语境紧密结合。旧日的采样片段以朦胧怀旧的质感重现，经过数字处理的人声在纹理中若隐若现。专辑既保留了vintage音色质感又避免了怀旧情绪，节奏不断变形、层次稀疏聚焦，呈现出持续向前的动态能量，在忧郁与活泼之间维持着张力。

items.excerpt: Review by Ctoro — Following his promising 2018 debut EP "Without Words," Samsworth once again proves he has the vision. items.body: Review by Ctoro — Following his promising 2018 debut EP "Without Words," Samsworth once again proves he has the vision. "Dream On" by Jon Samsworth stands out of the daring albums ever within the Canterbury scene, fully deconstructing its traditions while encapsulating its essence in his creation. Samsworth's effort is undeniably innovative and fearless, and, without question, the best authentic approach to the Canterbury scene at present. He dissects the Canterbury idiom to the avant-garde extreme in favor of revealing its dreamlike beauty. Jon Samsworth succeeded in that and for me "Dream On" the most organic yet experimental Canterbury music I've heard in years. This is his remarkable feat, making this album unique within the genre's framework - while simultaneously transcending it.All compositions are by Samsworth, supported by a large ensemble of talented musicians contributing a variety of instruments. Each brings their expertise and passion, layering the sound to create energetic, multi-faceted tracks. My personal favourite is "Topiary Exhedra with View of the Obelisk", named after an 18th-century painting by Balthazar Nebot depicting fanciful topiary imagined to have adorned Harwell House, Buckinghamshire. A live version is available on YouTube, performed by Samsworth on bass and digital harpsichord, with Malcolm Smith (piano), Ricardo Little (flute), Charlie Wickham (percussion) and Mary Holland (cello). Both versions have their own distinct appeal, offering different yet equally compelling interpretations. This piece ? and the album as a whole ? is a rare example of someone like Samsworth, hailing from Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire, embracing Canterbury scene heritage and presenting it in a form both grounded and innovative. It's a difficult balance to strike extremes within the genre framework, yet Samsworth navigates it effortlessly. "Dream On" offers a truly unique and offbeat listening experience rarely found elsewhere. If you're a fan of experimental and progressive music of any kind, I cannot recommend this album highly enough. Five stars.
items._genre: Canterbury scene / jazz fusion / avant-garde / experimental progressive
items._cn_summary: 这是Jon Samsworth继2018年首张EP后的第二张专辑《Dream On》，被乐评视为近年来对坎特伯雷场景最忠实也最具突破性的诠释。专辑大胆解构该流派传统语汇，将其推向先锋极端，同时保留其梦幻本质。所有曲目均由Samsworth本人作曲，邀约多位乐手参与，涵盖贝斯、数字大键琴、钢琴、长笛、打击乐与大提琴等多重编制，形成层次丰富、棱角分明的声场。乐评特别提及《Topiary Exhedra with View of the Obelisk》一曲，标题取自十八世纪画家Balthazar Nebot描绘白金汉郡Harwell House幻想园林的画作，录音室版与YouTube上的现场版各有侧重，前者由完整乐队编制呈现，后者回归贝斯与数字大键琴为核心的精简四人组配置。来自英格兰Aylesbury的Samsworth从本土视角拥抱坎特伯雷场景遗产，在极端实验与流派框架之间取得平衡，对前卫与实验音乐爱好者而言是一次难得的聆听体验。

items.album: Sauljaljui
items.excerpt: For the fourth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we head to a village room in southern Taiwan, where a group of Paiwan elders usually gather to sing their own folk songs. items.body: For the fourth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we head to a village room in southern Taiwan, where a group of Paiwan elders usually gather to sing their own folk songs. Into that room, one afternoon, walked a young metal drummer who had just moved home. Sauljaljui was back in Kapanan, her village in the Hengchun peninsula at Taiwan’s southern tip. Behind her were the university years, a nu-metal band, and a pile of rejected applications to Spring Scream, the festival every Taiwanese underground musician dreams of playing. She mentioned to an auntie that she still wanted to make music. The auntie said she knew somewhere… Old people’s music, she thought when the door opened onto a dozen elderly villagers with yueqin in their laps, the two-stringed Chinese moon lute, working through Paiwan songs she had never bothered to learn. She stayed anyway, pulled up a cajón, started holding the rhythm for them, and found they sang steadier for it. Soon she was playing every session, then performing with them, and they began treating her as one of their own grandchildren. It was only then, deep into that company, that she thought to ask one of the old women what she was actually singing about, and got back a memory from the woman’s childhood: a flower she’d spotted high on a cliff while playing hide-and-seek, too far up to pick, so she just stood and looked at it until the spring wind carried its scent down to her. She has said she felt ashamed and warmed at once. Folk music, it turned out, could be a way of singing the land itself, and she had been sitting in the room where it happened without hearing it. So she stopped keeping time for the elders and started learning from them, taking up the yueqin alongside the children of the village. Two strings, an instrument that had never belonged to her people, and somehow enough: she found her own idiom inside those constraints, folding in Austronesian rhythms gathered on tour and playing the lute as a rhythm section rather than a melodic voice. She sings mostly in Paiwan, a language spoken by fewer than 200,000 people and outlawed for years under colonial rule. And it was the elders, in the end, who put her on the Spring Scream stage her own band had never reached. That path led out of the village and a long way from it. Her self-produced 2025 album VAIVAIK, a title that means both searching and embarking in Paiwan, took Best Indigenous Language Album at Taiwan’s Golden Melody Awards, and its opening track “Dipin Kari Tang” took Best Arrangement. That one came out of a month she spent living and playing with musicians in Mauritius, and she recorded it with the Taiwu Ballads Troupe back home. She has worked for years inside Small Island Big Song too, which links Austronesian musicians across the Indo-Pacific around the ocean they hold in common. This October she brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, another island a long way from Kapanan. Below, she talks about the elders who taught her to sing, about carrying a language most of her audience will not understand, and about what she hopes to find on the island itself. She also curates a playlist of the tracks that shaped her sound, exclusively for Rhythm Passport. You’re bringing music that moved from heavy metal in college to Paiwan melodies rooted in your home village. For a WOMEX audience meeting you for the first time, how would you introduce that journey and the sound it led to? When I moved back to my hometown from the city to work, I met an auntie. I told her that I wanted to start a band and make music, so she took me somewhere. When I opened the door, I was surprised to see that everyone inside was elderly. They were playing the yueqin and singing traditional songs. At that time, I was honestly a little confused, because to me, it sounded like boring “old people’s music.” But after I joined them, I started playing the cajón to accompany them. In fact, with the rhythm of the cajón, they were able to sing together more steadily and in sync. Eventually, I started performing with them and accompanying their songs. One experience that really stayed with me was when we were invited to perform at Spring Scream, one of Taiwan’s most well-known music festivals. It’s a festival that almost every Taiwanese underground band dreams of playing. My own band had applied to Spring Scream many times, but we were never selected. Yet after I returned to my hometown, it was my grandparents from the village who brought me onto that stage. I remember standing backstage and teaching one of the grandpas how to make the “rocker” hand gesture when he went on stage. But when he got up there, he got it wrong and shouted, “Local!” instead. And somehow, the audience went even crazier! (Laughs) One day, I became curious and asked one of the grandmas, “What are the lyrics you’re singing about?” She told me about something that happened when she was a child. One day, while she was playing hide-and-seek, she saw a flower growing high up on a cliff. She wanted to pick it, but it was too far away. So she just kept looking at that flower. When the spring wind came, its fragrance carried into her heart. At that moment, I felt a little ashamed, but also deeply warmed. I realized that folk music could be a way of singing the land itself. As I spent more time with these elders, they began treating me like their own granddaughter. Being around them also made me softer and more gentle as a person. When I sang these songs with them, I felt like I was finally hearing my own true voice. It was as if I had found myself. You’ve said hearing your grandmother sing, a memory of flowers and spring wind carried in the words, changed how you understood what music could do. Does that moment still shape what you want a WOMEX showcase, and a room of strangers, to feel? I hope that when people listen to my music, they can imagine the place where I grew up, the land, the environment, the people, and the culture that have nurtured me. I believe they can hear that my music comes from somewhere real. It carries a kind of life force that has grown directly from the land. You brought the yueqin into Paiwan music by learning it alongside children in your village, even though it isn’t a traditional instrument for your people. Will it be part of what you bring to the WOMEX stage, and what does it let you do that a purely traditional set-up wouldn’t? The yueqin helped me break through creatively. It only has two strings, so there are obviously limitations to what you can do with it. But because of those limitations, I started asking myself how I could express who I am within that restricted space. I began combining the unique melodies of my own culture with the rhythms of Austronesian cultures that I encountered while traveling around the world. Over time, that became my own way of playing. So the yueqin is not just an instrument for me. It has become an important part of my musical language, and it will also be one of the main instruments I use in my performances. VAIVAIK means searching, or embarking, and the album is really about your own journey back to your language and your roots. What do you want a WOMEX audience, most of whom won’t know that story, to understand about that search when they hear it at your showcase? My culture has given me confidence. It taught me to truly believe that “tradition can be invented.” When I became brave enough to respond to my culture with my own ideas, rather than simply following what already existed, I finally felt a sense of openness within myself. It made my soul want to see the world. And now, I want to share that energy with the world without holding anything back. You’ve spoken about your father criticising your Paiwan, and feeling empty after your first award because you didn’t fully understand your own lyrics. Carrying the language to a WOMEX audience who won’t understand a word of it either, does that history change how you’ll sing it? Creating music in my native language naturally comes with its own challenges, especially because we have experienced colonization and the loss of our culture and language. But those difficulties don’t make me feel defeated. Instead, they give me strength. It’s okay if the audience doesn’t understand my language. When I stand on stage, I believe they can still feel the conviction and energy that I carry. Sometimes I think about what the world would be like if there were no language barriers. I believe what would remain is energy. And I believe the energy that my culture has given me can cross those language barriers and allow people to feel that life force. Small Island Big Song connected you with musicians across island cultures of the Indo-Pacific around the shared subject of the ocean. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is an island too, out in the Atlantic. Is there something about performing on another island, so far from your own, that you’re curious to explore there? I want to learn more about the history, people, culture, and environment of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. I’m also looking forward to experiencing the place beyond simply being there as a performer. I want to walk through the city, meet the people, and understand how this land lives and breathes. Your records fold Mauritian rhythms and jazz and rock in next to Paiwan tradition. In a WOMEX programme full of the world’s traditions, how do you want that mix to land, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? In the past, when I created music that involved cultural fusion, it was mostly about combining different musical styles. But “Dipin Kari Tang” was different. I lived there for a month, spending every day with local people, living together and jamming together. So this song wasn’t something I imagined from a distance. It came from a real experience and became part of me. In my culture, recognition and belonging can sometimes be more important than blood relations. If we recognize one another, then we are brothers and sisters. That’s the feeling I hope “Dipin Kari Tang” can bring to people. Even if we come from different places and different cultures, if we are willing to recognize and accept one another, we can become family. You’ve said people don’t need to remember your name, only your culture. WOMEX is built around industry attention on individual artists and their catalogues. How do you hold onto that idea in a room like that? I never imagined that one day I would step outside of myself through my music. For me, I’m really just a messenger, a person who carries and shares the things I believe in. And strangely, that gives me a sense of freedom. It’s something that exists on a spiritual level. At the same time, in the commercial world, I hope I can bring these two sides together, the spirit I believe in and my identity as a musician. I am Sauljaljui. I come from the Indigenous people of Taiwan. You wear a lot of different hats, singer, songwriter, teacher, festival organiser with KAPANAN back home. Beyond WOMEX, and maybe thanks to WOMEX, what’s next for you? This year, I bought a new van, and in September I’m going to start a van tour. I’ll be traveling to different Indigenous communities, spending about a month in each one, and sharing how my culture has guided me around the world and influenced my creative journey. I’ve been inspired by many people along the way, so now I want to walk into these communities myself and share what I’ve learned and experienced. I especially hope I can bring new ideas and courage to young people in the communities, and let them know that their culture doesn’t have to be a limitation. It can actually become the strength that allows us to go out into the world. If you could write a short, personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would you want them to know before they arrive? I’m Sauljaljui. Your long-lost half-sibling from another mother and another father. Come and listen to what I have to say   This October, Sauljaljui carries the songs of the Paiwan elders who taught her, and the two-stringed moon lute she learned beside them, onto the stage at WOMEX in Las Palmas     PLAYLIST: SAULJALJUJ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Sauljaljui appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: Sauljaljui 的专辑 VAIVAIK 以台湾排湾族语言演唱，将月琴作为节奏声部而非旋律载体，融入南岛语系跨域节奏。这张作品诞生于一个反叙事：一位曾玩新金属的年轻鼓手回到南部村庄，偶然进入长者聚会，从替老人打节拍到真正聆听歌词中关于土地的记忆。专辑与毛里求斯音乐人合作一个月后回乡录制，将岛屿之间的对话压缩进排湾古谣的骨架。评述聚焦于她如何从被殖民禁用的语言中重新提炼音乐性，以及为何两弦乐器足以承载整个南岛语系的海洋叙事。这张作品获得台湾金曲奖最佳原住民语专辑，其首曲 Dipin Kari Tang 获最佳编曲。

items.body: Label: Nonesuch Records, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute; Vijay Iyer: piano; Dafnis Prieto: drums. Henry Threadgill, a living legend, avant-garde jazz eminence, and master composer, joins forces with the incredibly creative pianist Vijay Iyer, a reference in modern creative jazz, and proficient Cuban-born drummer Dafnis Prieto, who has worked with Arturo O'Farrill, Eddie Palmieri, and John Zorn. Their debut trio album, Fifteen , comprises a strangely addictive set of post-modern and avant-garde tunes—three by both Threadgill and Iyer, and two by Prieto—that are easily recommended for fans of the three musicians. The album title refers to the number of years the trio has been performing together. Threadgill's " Trio Piece " opens the curtain in a cerebral, slow-chugging way, placing ethereal flute over mystery-inducing piano textures set in the lower register, with understated drumming punctuated by occasional syncopation. If this track gives you an idea of what comes next, " Last Night ", also composed by Threadgill, exceeds our expectations. Boasting a great vibe via its obtuse groove, the piece thrives with forward-leaning drumming, tart saxophone lines, and angular pianism. In the same feral grip of extravagance and sense of groove, Iyer's " I Wanted a Map " mixes structural rock groundwork, avant-garde literacy, and even a bit of Americana. Threadgill blows with soul on the latter, switching to flute on Prieto's " Gently Trapped ", where we can sense a classical innuendo in Iyer's playing. An ethereal flow and an agreeably smooth texture are defining characteristics of this piece. In turn, Iyer's " Fire City " goes from ruminative to ebullient, entering full explorative mode. The theme revealed at the end feels intensely bright yet typified by a few shadowy spots. Blending acute teamwork and killer textures, the trio is free to explore harmonically in the way Iyer envisioned. Yet on his pathos-packed " Perfect Victims ", he rightfully opts for simply arpeggiated sequences that further enhance its elegiac tones. In addition to wailing alto sax, we have timely cymbal washes turned thunderous tom-tom mechanics, providing a ricocheting sense of dynamism at the end. Prieto's " On the Way " packs a wallop, proving the drummer to be a skilled composer. There's a Latin freshness to it, while still bringing out Threadgill's stylistic parameters. Galvanizing percussive work, bustling piano arrays, and terse saxophone expression — all contribute to the hip swagger. This adventurous trio with a distinctly individual vibe certainly has its inventive ways of making its music sound interesting. Fifteen encompasses three strong compositional voices, leading to superior results. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Last Night ► 03 - I Wanted a Map ► 04 - Gently Trapped ► 08 - On the Way
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是三位音乐家合作十五年后的首张三重奏录音作品，包含九首原创曲目。Threadgill 的作品以低沉钢琴音色为底，叠加空灵长笛与含蓄鼓点，慢节奏展开充满沉思感；Iyer 的曲目融合摇滚结构、前卫语汇与美洲音乐元素，钢琴与萨克斯在不同情绪间自如切换，从内省到爆发；Prieto 的作品展现其作为作曲家的实力，带有拉丁色彩。三位音乐家各有独立的作曲声音，在即兴中保持敏锐的团队互动，音响层次丰富，结构严谨又不失自由探索的空间。

items._cn_summary: 巴黎音响艺术家尼亚姆克·迪吉尔的第三张专辑，延续其以田野录音为核心的创作脉络。作品取材于加纳故土之旅采集的环境声响，与小提琴展开音乐对话，制作过程中刻意剔除打击乐元素，引导听者聚焦于音色的持续延展与空间层次。由此构建的音响世界横跨环境音乐、噪音与无人机三大类型边界，深邃而辽阔。田野录音与器乐即兴的融合使作品脱离了传统欧洲实验音乐的文本逻辑，注入非洲大陆的声音质感与文化记忆，形成跨地域的声学对话。整体呈现出沉稳、内省且具有地理纵深感的听觉体验。

items.excerpt: ミネアポリスのマックス・デヴロー。1994年生まれの彼が2026年に日本のコジマ録音からリリースしたアルバム『レジスタンス』は1本のエレキギターを用いて5つのテーマを通じて極めてノイジーで尖鋭的な響きの探究を試みている。作品はあらゆる楽器で演奏可能なオープン・ワークとして構想されており、ブックレットにはそれぞれの楽曲の図形譜が付属している。今年1月、彼が暮らすミネアポリスでD. トランプと彼が率いるICEによって引き起こされ三千人以上の逮捕者を出した大規模な非正規移民の拘束と強制送還作戦〈メトロ・サージ作戦〉の騒乱と混沌を音楽的に記録した1枚でもある。

items._cn_summary: 1994年出生的美国明尼阿波利斯音乐人Max Devereaux，于2026年通过日本小厂牌Kojima录音发行专辑《レジスタンス》。整张作品仅使用一把电吉他，围绕五个主题展开，对极度嘈杂而尖锐的声响进行深入探索。作品被构想为可用任何乐器演奏的开放性文本，乐谱以图形谱形式附于册页中。专辑同时是对2026年1月明尼阿波利斯本地由D.特朗普及其领导的ICE所发动的〈Metro Surge行动〉大规模骚乱与混沌的音乐记录，三千余人因此被逮捕并遭强制遣返。作品将政治现实转化为声音实验，以单件乐器承载社会动荡的听觉叙事。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / electronic / East African folk / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕独立厂牌 Cool Waters 发行，是德国裔肯尼亚打击乐手 Sven Kacirek 与83岁传统肯尼亚歌手 Ogoya Nengo 以及合作搭档 Olith Ratengo 的首次三方录音。评论着重分析了几首作品的声音层次：合成器极简节拍开场，逐步叠加四拍律动、低音线条与木琴音色，使电子合成节奏与原声人声在不知不觉中融为一体；另一首曲目中，失真音效在演唱高潮处悄然浮现，强化了情感张力。文中将其置于当代跨文化协作的语境中，与海地 Chouk Bwa 等团体的"民间电子化"路径相提并论，指出这类作品的特殊价值在于：既保持非洲传统根源的深度，又以电子手段拓展前卫表达，使古老的歌唱传统与合成器节奏共存而不互相压制。83岁歌手的全球首秀与白人电子音乐人的合作，被视为这种边界模糊化的典型例证。

Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,

Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑以自制乐器为核心特色，乐手用废旧物品手工打造了所谓的 tassofons、kitchenofon 等非常规乐器，这些自制品在录音中呈现出惊人的音准和饱满音质。专辑将多种世界音乐风格编织在一起：开场曲融入克莱兹默传统，笑声般的单簧管搭配巴松管和急促打击乐；'Le Cuenta' 转向昆比亚风格，长笛与拉丁打击乐交织；同名曲营造非洲节拍氛围，木鱼和沙锤散布于混音中；'Ambiguidade' 呈现桑巴律动，'Aksum' 则勾勒出中东迷幻色彩。每首曲目都安排了即兴段落，演奏者展现出扎实的技术功底。专辑不仅是音乐作品，也是对'如何用最简陋的材料创造音乐'这一命题的实践，呼应了全球文化中节奏与旋律的共通性。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Camilla Hole Trio继前作将科幻合成器音色与传统民间素材嫁接之后推出的新作，整体回归更为朴素的地面感。专辑以Soprano Sax为核心，融合Double Bass、鼓、模块合成器与颤音琴，演奏中成员角色不断流动，乐器之间的旋律与节奏功能持续互换。以挪威西部民间舞曲Springleik为代表的曲目起始于传统旋律的陈述，随后逐步展开即兴段落，Hole的萨克斯、Kalman的低音旋律线与Nesheim的开放式节奏层层推进，结构松散而充满对话感。整体呈现北欧民间素材与自由爵士即兴思维的深度交融，对偏好实验与世界音乐交汇的听众具有相当的吸引力。
