items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — France has always been a land of revolutions, ranging from the political to the musical. The French had their own way of assimilating various foreign currents, adapting them to their own unique character. They did this with classic jazz, featuring musicians such as Michel Legrand, St�phane Grappelli, and Django Reinhardt (who, despite being Belgian, spent the majority of his career in France), and later by adopting jazz-rock fusion into their style, as exemplified by Jean-Luc Chevalier, a guitarist born in the Cholet region of France in 1948. In fact, Magma, Christian Vander's band, incorporated numerous fusion elements and featured Chevalier from 1978 to 1984.When he joined Magma, everything clicked perfectly; it wasn't just a matter of the style suiting his own. As Chevalier himself often maintained, what mattered was the "spirit," not pretentious intellectualism. He would often say that a track like John McLaughlin's "Guardian Angel" must have been composed in a trance-like state, driven by the energy of the moment. Chevalier used to say that Jeff Beck, Jaco Pastorius, Christian Vander, and Hendrix were not "armchair intellectuals," and that, precisely for this reason, that kind of contamination did not exist in Magma.With Magma, he played not only the guitar but also the bass, and, as he himself maintained, it was about intense emotions, about unleashing a hidden madness. He maintained a long-standing relationship, spanning many years, with percussionist Jean Chevalier (known as "Popoff"), who had joined Zig Zag in 1972 and with whom he would form various duos and trios. In the early 1980s, he formally launched his solo career, performing in a trio alongside Bertrand Renaudin and Marc Eliard for the album Un pied dans le vide (1985), a work that featured an experimental vibe reminiscent of Mike Stern's early period (wild and fast-paced), as well as an ethnic spirit that permeated the recording.Paradoxe N�II calls to mind the pyrotechnic John McLaughlin of the pre-Mahavishnu era, when?even within the seemingly stripped-down jazz trio format, the sound could feel as though it were floating in space. Meanwhile, on L'Abandon, the guitar doubles the very same keyboard riffs typical of jazz fusion. Amiti�s et encore builds a melody, and in this regard, it also draws a parallel to Pat Metheny, who could improvise and experiment without ever losing sight of the harmonic and melodic direction."Baillou Pack Pack" features the electric bass driving a distinctly funk-oriented sound, while Chevalier's guitar work, incorporating distinctly Arabic-style solos, lends itself to extended improvisation; the track then shifts into a rock style, undergoing a dramatic stylistic metamorphosis, all within a single song.In "Concerto Grosso," percussion plays a pivotal role, and the nylon-string guitar provides a warm tone reminiscent of Baden Powell, who was living in Europe at the time, occasionally veering into dissonance and pushing boundaries in the same spirit as the Brazilian master."L'abrozo" continues the fusion with a highly recognizable bassline but a restless guitar, initially adopting a Robert Fripp-esque "Frippertronics" style before shifting into atmospheric jazz that the guitarist himself proceeds to distort, all while the rhythm section accelerates and decelerates in support. In any case, it's impossible not to tap your feet."Un pied dans le vide", the title track, appears at the end for a very good reason: it is epic. The melody is unusual for a fusion album; indeed, coming from a French guitarist schooled by Christian Vander, nothing could be predictable. Infernal, dark notes erupt from the guitar, while the drums and bass provide the wind that allows that "bird", his guitar, to take flight. There are echoes of King Crimson, uncommon for a fusion record, and one might even be reminded of the band Present, until a sophisticated atmosphere reminiscent of a French police procedural or film noir takes over the song, maintaining that same sense of mystery.During his time with Magma, Chevalier adopted the name Wurd Gorgo (in the style of Gong members) which meant something akin to "The Demon Gorgo" in Koba�an mythology. In doing so, he delved into the unfathomable depths of the spirit of his discography, inviting us to join him in that journey.
items._cn_summary: 这张1985年的专辑由法国吉他手Jean-Luc Chevalier录制，他在Magma乐队时期积累了丰富的融合经验。作品以爵士三重奏为基底，吉他、贝斯与打击乐之间展开密集对话，风格跨越多个领域：既有Mike Stern早期那种狂野快速的实验气质，也融入Pat Metheny式的旋律意识。阿拉伯风格独奏与世界音乐元素贯穿始终，与传统硬波普形成对比；尼龙弦吉他在部分曲目中带来接近Baden Powell的温暖质感，偶尔滑向不和谐音。鼓击段落承担结构性功能，电子贝斯推动放克律动，吉他则在单首作品中完成从东方音阶到摇滚爆发力的剧烈风格转变。整体上这是一张拒绝学院化、强调即兴能量与精神驱动的法式融合作品，介于前卫实验与世界音乐融合之间。

items.body: Goetia is a Turkish band I hadn’t heard of before. I discovered that they have released four singles since last year and are now launching their debut album, “Saligia”, featuring seven tracks -dealing with the 7 deadly sins. Incidentally, the four previously released singles are also included on the album. Their influences clearly lie within the broad realm of EBM. While the tracks remain rudimentary and minimal in their composition, some feature appealing, icy sounds. This is a fine example of a band getting the absolute most out of limited resources. The best proof of this is the track “Haris”, which stands out significantly and packs more punch than the other songs. Another distinctive feature of the production is that the vocals are delivered in their native language, with the exception of one German passage. Goetia certainly still has some work to do when it comes to the overall mix and production, but “Saligia” already sounds quite good and, above all, promising. I look forward to seeing what comes next. (Rating:7). Listen to “Haris”: Haris by Goetia About Goetia Goetia is a darkwave band based in Ankara, Türkiye, working around themes of occultism, inner conflict, and existential decay. The band combines darkwave, EBM, and industrial elements into a cold, immersive sound built on hypnotic rhythms, analog-inspired synthesizers, and minimal structures. Music and production on the group’s material are credited to Berent Oral and Tolgahan Pehlivanlı, with Pehlivanlı also handling lyrics, vocals, and mixing. A founding date has not been confirmed. Goetia released four singles ahead of its debut album: “Esans”, “Nihil”, “Döngü”, and “Nektar”. The band’s debut full-length, “Saligia”, followed on April 3, 2026 through Tamar Records. The title is a Latin acronym for the seven deadly sins (Superbia, Avaritia, Luxuria, Invidia, Gula, Ira, Acedia), and the seven-track album is built around that theme, with mastering by Uğur Yelkenci and cover artwork by Nuryağmur Candar.
items._cn_summary: Goetia 是一支来自土耳其安卡拉的暗潮/EBM乐队，首张专辑《Saligia》以七首曲目对应七宗罪的主题展开。音乐融合暗潮、EBM与工业元素，核心特征为冷峻沉浸的氛围、催眠式律动、模拟质感的合成器音色与极简结构编制。歌曲主要由土耳其语演唱，仅有一段德语歌词，形成独特的语言质感。制作人 Berent Oral 与 Tolgahan Pehlivanlı 以有限资源实现最大化效果，混音与整体制作仍有提升空间，但单曲《Haris》展现了乐队最具冲击力的面貌。专辑由 Tamar Records 于 2026 年 4 月发行，母带处理与封面设计均完成度高。乐评认为作品已具备相当完成度且前景可期。

items._cn_summary: 这张1979年现场录音的再发版记录了无国籍音乐团体俄勒冈在魁北克与纽约的演出实况。该团由保罗·温特在六十年代后期创立，成员流动，以原声爵士为根基融合古典与世界音乐元素，跨越数十年仍保持独特美学。拉尔夫·唐纳等乐手以ECM系独奏与合奏作品闻名，在此呈现的现场演出充满即兴对话与细腻声响层次。安静氛围、纤细音色与紧张感交织成庄严空间，形成多层次变化的世界观，体现出不衰的吸引力。作为长寿命组合的现场实况记录，它忠实呈现了团队独特的合奏语言与即兴互动方式。

items.body: Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. Contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed Incompleteness by Kid Bucle   I have humbly decided that this extended player affords me a slightly self-indulgent opportunity to locate myself within a lineage of which I can only ever claim to be a fragment. Or at least, the Incompleteness is so good, it’s triggered a reflective expression. Regardless, here we are. By the latter half of the 1990s, the UK underground party scene had become a sprawling ecosystem of overlapping futures. We were listening and dancing to top-tier releases from Underground Resistance, Jeff Mills, Transmat, Aril Brikha, The Jedi Knights, Dave Angel and, inevitably, Aphex Twin; elsewhere tracing the Detroit lineage through artists such as Drexciya, Dopplereffekt, Stasis et al, while the years around the turn of the century brought everything from Legowelt to LA Synthesis. Ian O’Brien, and Swayzak into our mixes. Alongside all this, an apparently endless procession of mutations and crossovers moved between techno(s) and house(s)—much of which would later be flattened, retrospectively packaged and homogenized beneath the convenient umbrella of tech house. But our lived reality was considerably less tidy than the history books might suggest. Genres were still adventurous and porous. Scenes were still arguing with themselves. New sounds arrived before anyone had decided what to call them. And beneath the increasingly polished surface of the decade’s mainstream culture, something else was happening. The countercultural and artistic momentum inherited from earlier generations had not disappeared; it had dispersed. As the millennium approached—with all the absurdly romantic anxiety of a fabricated timestamp promising either technological transcendence or digital collapse—another current began to gather force. For those of us becoming desensitised to the necessary but increasingly familiar four-to-the-floor grammar of house and techno, another possibility was emerging: a renewed electro futurism that felt less like revival than reactivation. There were already telling fractures in the beat. Breakbeat had changed the landscape. Broken beat, trip hop and electronica had widened the vocabulary. And when we went out, we wanted something fast, digital, electronic and funky enough to make the body move without requiring it to march. Something that excited the central nervous system and that spoke to the parameters of our escapist fugue states. UR003 was a mainstay. “Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet.” ~Will Wonks Such electro became cool again because, for a while, it seemed to offer an escape from the routine of clubbing routines. The second generation unwittingly arrived carrying the DNA of the pioneers but operating within a newly expanded electronic landscape. Carl Finlow. Anthony Rother. Sons of Slough. Scopex Records. Tipper. Spacetime Continuum all flirted with or championed nu-skool electro. As well as a million other unsung operators, each extending and corrupting the signal. Their work reimagined the pioneering futurism of Kraftwerk alongside the electro-funk detonations of Bambaataa, Hashim‘s Al-Naafiysh, Juan Atkins‘ Cybotron and Soul Sonic Force, YMO, Thomas Dolby, Moroder, and on. The result was not a revival. It was a reprogramming: a music that understood its ancestry while refusing to remain obedient to it. And that mattered because the consequences extended far beyond electro itself. That late-90s emergence contained the seed of the genre hybridisation we now take for granted: the willingness to let one vocabulary contaminate another, to treat genre less as a boundary than a component. Twenty-five years later, the descendants are everywhere. From glitch, Vapourwave, Chiptune, and experimental sound design pursued almost for its own sake, through braindance and Drill into the innumerable hybrid forms that followed, the electronic underground has become increasingly less concerned with preserving distinctions than discovering what happens when those distinctions are deliberately ignored. Of course, in the end there are not really two seasons of electro music—before and after, old and new. There is only the thread and the evolutionary impulses across it. A single, constantly mutating continuum that survives precisely because it is repeatedly pulled apart and reassembled as we explore, as we progressively commit to a healthy artistic development, backed up against an almost cataclysmic regression as a total species. That evolutionary thread remains alive now in the work orbiting labels such as CPU, Frustrated Funk, Analogical Force, Lunar Disko, Semantica; artists such as Annie Hall, Fleck E.S.C., Plant 43, Scape One, and here, the numerous entrants within the Science Cult ecosystem—my apologies to the innumerable others omitted here in the interests of eventually getting to the point. What connects them is not simply a sound. It is a commitment to beats and textures as an ongoing unfinished technology; to the idea that electronic music can still be strange, physical, funny, brutal, sophisticated and forward-facing all at once. That it remembers its roots as we subjectively forget. Any sufficiently deep study of art eventually reveals two competing pulses within the creative whorl. One is inheritance: the necessity of what has come before, its vocabulary and accumulated possibilities. The other is departure: the impulse to misuse that vocabulary in order to discover what else it might become. Both are necessary because both ultimately serve the same purpose—to express what is, right here, right now. Then there are the anomalies. The pioneers who, for a brief period at least, appear to operate without discernible reference points; artists whose internal cosmology is so singular that influence becomes difficult to map until everybody else catches up. Aphex Twin is an obvious example for our purposes. Such figures are rare. They are timestamps rather than trends. Archetypes, if you like: creative appearances through which something enters the culture and leaves a mark durable enough to outlive its moment. It is not for me to say here whether Kid Bucle (aka Valencia, Spain-based Malsum — Ibrahim Pedernera Martinez) belongs amongst such company. Nor, really, is it the job of a review to make that kind of proclamation. No objective assessment can supersede direct subjective experience. But perhaps one purpose of this indulgent preamble is to establish the territory into which this Incompleteness release newly arrives—and to make it absolutely clear that the effort being expended here is inspired entirely by the music itself. Because finally, this is about the music. Nothing else. Incompleteness then, is a forward-facing kick in the proverbial: a prototypical experimental experience that moves in, out, around and through what we might loosely describe as electro’s most progressive potential. It does so without sounding particularly interested in protecting the borders of electro in the first place. There is a bias towards increased tempo and a natural disposition towards the collapse of genre itself—for want of a better term, post-genre. The constituent elements of electronic music are all present, but they have been liberated (obliterated?) from their traditional obligations. Tops and bottoms. Breadth and depth. Width and height. Rhythm, texture, melody and impact are scattered across the stereo field like components from several different machines forced to cooperate. The programming is scattergun, intricate and frequently exhilarating. The digi-breaks are unapologetically funkapolian. Yet beneath the technical complexity lies an innate musicality: atmosphere, timbre and cinematic texture are not decorative additions but structural components. This is music with a stank-faced sense of awe about it. One listen’s partly in admiration and partly in disbelief that someone has managed to keep so many moving parts from tearing the entire thing apart, whilst still landing in majesty and beauty. Art that hits the spot in the listener it appeared at in its creator. “Parasitos” opens the EP with precisely that tendency towards atmosphere. Broken electronic architecture stutters and strafes, evolving and mutating through vaguely Eastern folk motifs, tearing bass and binary science. Dust-and-musk textures collide with braindance-adjacent chopped Amen snares, occasionally summoning the restless imagination of early (Sony) Tipper without ever settling into anything near imitation. It is a beautifully brutal dalliance between effort and instinct, a near-perfect amalgam of technical obsession and artistic purpose. This is an electronic wonk at work inside the digital framework of contemporary electronic production—and every decision appears to have enduring consequences. “Space Feedback” is something else again. Nothing feels absent. Nothing feels superfluous. Every bolt and bough appears to have been considered, as though a bomb is being meticulously dismantled, tenderly rebuilt and then deliberately detonated anyway. It is perhaps the purest embodiment of everything this review is struggling to describe with far too many words. Broken electro structures buckle against stuttering, hard-funked woob bass; summer-warm pads provide unexpected emotional oxygen to create clean air between the mechanical clanks and insectoid impacts. The sheer finesse here is delicious. Music more than worth the cost to both composer and audience. This is, arguably, quite simply, a classic in waiting. Title track, “Incompleteness,” opens with something approaching a Villeneuve-ian majesty. Monumental synth grandeur and bubbling acid stabs occupy an immense cinematic space before the next wave of thundering rhythm begins to tenderly pound both inside and outside the implied loop. Formation and collapse coalesce in abandon. Systems establish themselves only to be interrupted by their own malfunction. It is difficult not to hear the labour in the work—not in the sense of something overworked, but because the time, technique and attention are inscribed directly into the sound. Whether innate or learned is beside the point. The skill is unapologetically on display. It is an extraordinary piece of contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed. “Decipher” takes the closing-credits position and, true to the spirit of the EP, refuses merely to repeat what has gone before. The opportunity to say something different—to demonstrate range, shade and alternative possibility—is grasped with both hands. Thundering, rolling tribal rhythms rumble beneath high-octane strings and expansive pads, while percussive refrains and double-time synthesizer arpeggios build further cinematic dimensions around the forming rhythms. There is a wonderful sense of musicality here, almost of scoring: the feeling that the music is accompanying images we have not yet seen. And perhaps that is the achievement of Incompleteness as an apparently single release set among the routines of too many others. It understands the continuum without becoming trapped by it. Its references are not a museum of influences but raw material. The past is present only insofar as it can still be made useful. Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. There is rare bravery in that. There is serious technique. More importantly, here there is absolute joy. The glory of art in full effect. Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet. This EP is an unequivocal 10/10 proposition. Incompleteness is available on Science Cult. items._cn_summary: 这张EP将90年代末英国地下俱乐部场景中futurism、tek-funk与碎裂机器声响的脉络延伸至当代语境，以碎拍节奏、电子合成与数字音色构建出快速、紧凑而又保持身体律动感的作品。作者将其置于底特律techno谱系与broken beat、trip hop的交汇点上，强调那种不需整齐四拍、却能激发中枢神经的逃逸状态。整张EP对电子音乐本身的"未完成性"保持自觉：不追求完备的闭合结构，而是以突变、断裂和未被命名的声音持续试探机器内部尚未被触及的可能性。评论将其视为当代电子艺术中既具身体性又兼具细节密度的一次推进。

items.body: Made your hell from the fire inside Played in flames that burned you alive What went through your head when you lost your mind The true tragedy is the world decides Something ancient in the crowd gathers around a famous death. A murder becomes spectacle; strangers study photographs, motives, wounds, and final moments as though proximity to horror might grant some secret knowledge. The macabre is easiest to enjoy when the dead are unknown to us, when grief belongs to another household and blood has no familiar name. Tragedy, then, can be consumed as theater, mystery, even entertainment. We call it curiosity, but often it is appetite dressed in respectable clothes. Civilization may depend, in part, on remembering that every spectacle was first a human life actually lived. We’ve seen it played out countless times in real life, as well as in profound films like Day of the Locust. Seattle goth dance-punk trio Holy Death Temple return with their fourth single, Nobody Loved You, a murder ballad that is shamelessly poppy and driven by a fiery bassline and fierce drumming that make the song feel almost indecently buoyant. Bryan Edward’s programming gives the track the clean immediacy of gothic synth-pop, while Jon Barrysmith’s drums keep the floor moving beneath it. Wren Rose folds guitar, synth, and backing vocals into the arrangement without crowding the hook. Edward handles lead vocals, guitar, and programming; Barrysmith (Year of the Cobra, Rifflord) takes drums; Rose (Broken Focus) supplies guitar, synth, and backing vocals. There is a little Sisters of Mercy gloom in the DNA, some Depeche Mode pop precision, and enough dance-punk velocity to place Holy Death Temple comfortably alongside ACTORS, Sextile, and VR SEX. Nobody Loved You finds its real character in the gap between what the body hears and what the lyrics are saying. The song examines the public appetite that gathers around violent death, particularly the urge to turn murder into a referendum on character. Someone dies, and almost immediately spectators begin sorting themselves into camps, prosecuting the dead, defending the killer, reconstructing motives, and deciding who deserved what. Condemnation becomes a recreational drug with excellent engagement numbers. The man at the center of the lyrics is controlling, cruel, hungry for power, and shaped by abandonment that eventually curdles into brutality. His wife endures pain and sacrifice until the arrangement ends with death. Holy Death Temple lets the listener enjoy condemning him for a while, then complicates that satisfaction by asking why everyone becomes so obsessed with determining whether a death was justified while showing far less interest in how a human being arrived at such a miserable destination. That question feels particularly sharp in an age where high-profile killings become participatory entertainment, complete with amateur detectives, moral tribunals, leaked photographs, podcast episodes, TikTok theories, and millions of strangers inspecting somebody else’s catastrophe from bed. Bryan Edward seems fully aware of how strange it is to package all of this inside something so catchy: “Never thought we’d explore our fascination with high-profile murders and repressed Erasure influence in the same song, but here we are,” he quips. “…Nobody Loved You is a mercy-killed synth-pop demo resurrected with a hook intended for a completely different track. Our best moments come from botched experiments and happy accidents.” Listen to Nobody Loved You below and order the single here. Nobody Loved You by Holy Death Temple Nobody Loved You is a bright synth-pop ‘mistake’ with a body in the trunk, built for the dance floor while staring straight at one of civilization’s uglier appetites: the thrill of death when the grief belongs to somebody else. items._cn_summary: 西雅图暗潮三人组Holy Death Temple带来第四首单曲《Nobody Loved You》，一首谋杀民谣形式的哥特合成器流行作品。Bryan Edward负责主唱、吉他与编程，Jon Barrysmith担任鼓手，Wren Rose贡献吉他、合成器与和声。编曲以干净利落的合成器质感为基底，强劲贝斯线与炽热鼓点驱动出近乎不道德的轻快感，整体呈现出Sisters of Mercy式阴郁气质与Depeche Mode流行精准度的融合，并具备足够的舞曲后朋克速度感。歌词层面，作品聚焦于公众围绕暴力死亡的围观欲望，审视社会如何将谋杀转化为道德审判与娱乐消费，质问人们为何热衷于判定死亡是否正义，却鲜少追问一个人如何走向毁灭。作品在身体感受的愉悦与文本所揭示的残酷之间制造张力，邀请听众先享受谴责，再反思这种满足本身。

items.body: Hands in the sky and then we die Our hearts have joined the thousand We take a step into the night Opening our eyes brings a new dawn The Goth subculture has survived for nearly half a century partly because every few years somebody remembers that death can be absurd. Strip away that humour and the genre starts resembling a homeowners’ association for people with excellent boots: approved haircuts, approved records, approved photographs taken beside approved statues in approved cemeteries. Then Comes Silence have enough mileage behind them to recognize the danger. Remaker Redeemer finds the Stockholm trio Alex Svenson, Jonas Fransson, and Hugo Zombie treating the graveyard as a playground again. Then Comes Silence fortunately remembers that a black shirt is still a shirt. The album itself is conceived as a diptych, with “Requiem” representing darkness and “Ballroom” representing light. “Everything exists in contrast,” the band says. Remaker Redeemer introduces the “Ballroom” half of the band’s forthcoming Requiem Ballroom, due November 20. The band explains that the song “is about new life, being reborn with old sins washed away. A kind of cleansing, a fresh start, and the feeling of beginning again. The choice of instruments and sounds on this track was also a way to explore something a bit different this time.” Svenson’s bass plants every movement firmly beneath the feet, while Fransson’s drums drive the song with a dark, danceable force reminiscent of Killing Joke’s Night Time era. Svenson’s grave, commanding vocals strengthen the comparison, while Zombie’s guitar cuts through with a bright, sharp edge. There is genuine pleasure in the performance, closer to liberation than solemn contemplation, which suits a song concerned with starting over. Rebirth here apparently requires amplification, eyeliner, and several people dressed as failed medical experiments. The song’s lyrics treat death as a passage toward renewal, moving from surrender and darkness toward another existence. Closed eyes, raised hands, joined hearts, and the arrival of dawn suggest a collective transformation, while the repeated call to a remaker and redeemer turns rebirth into an act of cleansing: old sins washed away, one life surrendered, and another beginning on the other side. The video makes the album’s concept pleasantly mischievous. Renewal takes place among monsters. Cleansing occurs in a room full of freaks. Life returns while death watches from the front row. Directed by Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films, the video places the band before a congregation of ghouls, Droogs, demons, grotesques, and evil babies. Yes, evil babies that look like escapees from the bargain bin of some forbidden 1970s horror shop, which immediately gives the clip more personality than another five minutes of serious men staring into industrial fog. Zurawski photographs the performance beautifully while allowing the absurdity to breathe. Svenson holds court on bass and vocals with severe composure while Fransson hammers away behind him and Zombie sends guitar across the room in sharp strokes. Around them, the assembled creatures stare, convulse, leer, and generally behave like the clientele of a nightclub whose liquor license was issued by Satan. Watch the video for Remaker Redeemer below: Rock music periodically develops the delusion that dignity equals importance, an especially fatal mistake for any subculture born from makeup, theatrical clothing, cheap smoke machines, horror films, and teenagers trying to scandalize their parents. The original punk impulse understood spectacle as provocation. Somewhere along the road, certain corners of underground culture began treating their uniforms with the solemnity of military dress. That final joke may be the best one. Subcultures survive through mutation, bad taste, risk, exaggeration, and people willing to make fools of themselves in public. Then Comes Silence understands that preservation without mischief eventually becomes embalming. Remaker Redeemer puts the corpse back on its feet, gives it a bass guitar, and lets the evil babies dance. Then Comes Silence are currently on tour in mainland Europe. items._cn_summary: Then Comes Silence 以三件套编制在《Remaker Redeemer》中呈现出鲜明的哥特后朋克气质。贝斯线条稳健扎实，鼓机式的鼓组提供暗黑而具舞蹈感的驱动力，电吉他音色锐利明亮，人声低沉而威严，整体气质可追溯至 Killing Joke《Night Time》时期的阴郁仪式感。专辑以二联画形式构思，“Requiem”代表黑暗、“Ballroom”代表光明，歌曲本身探讨死亡、重生与净化，旧罪洗去、新生开启的主题贯穿歌词。 MV 导演 Zurawski 将表演置于怪物、恶婴与畸形人偶之中，赋予作品荒诞而戏谑的视觉个性，区别于严肃工业迷雾的套路。整张作品将仪式感与幽默并置，让哥特亚文化重新成为游戏而非教条。

items.body: Chris Dooks – Accretion Disc The LP by Chris Dooks begins with some lovely brass, augmented by trails of chiming choral voice. “Sorry I was just carrying this”, a voice explains, pointing to the idea that Dooks is carrying a voice recorder between destinations. The meshing of found sounds and recorded material is admirable. “I went to work once” a baby talks to the man holding the device, having a conversation with her about baby steps. Just by listening there is a possibility of auditory hallucination between ages and genders, as if either vocabulary could be stated for either subject. The second track also starts well, introducing fuzzy, smoothly-dappled drones into the organic/synthetic wash of sound. It’s a mix and a wash, like a soundtrack to an underwater ferris wheel attraction powered by the whistles on the wind. Indeed there is a whistling melody from the synth to summon in the tide, sounding like a reprise to Goldfrapp’s “Horse Tears”, released on Mute in 2000. Pretty sonic colours fill the mind with a churning drone effusion that could be the soundtrack to some Legend Of Zelda game from afar. It can be stated by hereon in that ‘Accretion’ turns into an expansive and peacing ambient record equal parts The Caretaker in ballroom style opera samples (the third track) and the tired yawning hums throughout. They do not dull the listener into a false sense of security; neither do they disconcert in the blight of anxiety. All in accretion is for good and bad, and there’s more good here than anything else. Jason Van Wyk – Attachment The second Eilean Rec. release added to the roster for March is by Jason Van Wyk, a very Goldmund-calibre composer using acoustic piano, drone strings and bittersweet candyfloss atmospheres to paint a Nest-reaching path towards and past hope and regret. “Attachment LP” opener “Kept” is initially desolate and soul searching, but not searing, like a bad breakup of vows or orders in the mind. Thoughtfulness underlines itself on Jason’s compositional standard. Like Chris Dooks album, the opener is merely a bookend, a prologue of sorts. Much is to be revealed by investment. Second piece, “Before” is veering fuller into filmic worlds and imagined shadow lands, a pulse outlined on the brink of regulation ebbing and flowing like a shark bobbing underwater, evading a human captor. The important hinge in the pathbetween organic and inorganic sound here and storyline is that Van Wyk shows unnatural sounds are not always dangerous sounds. This is also a key component of the release, kicking the listener on gently with a little push instead of a fatalblow. That quality – the ability to restrain the overarching weight of the classical string – is complimentarily treatedand tempered by the piano flourishes that pitter and patter in a well of resonant melodic rain. Rain and refrain, as such composite syllable associations, is comparable to the structural density of this recording by Jason. Raining and refraining from destroying and abstaining as well curate the theme of this review of Eilean material -will o’ the wisp in execution, timelessly orchestrated instrumentally and indispensible as such, these would be two lovely discs or records/downloads for anyone’s family archive. www.eilean-records.com

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了十三支比利时乐团的作品，录制于1129年建立的鲁汶郊外帕克修道院。修道院石质空间提供的天然混响成为专辑的沉默合伙人，塑造出温暖而沉思的整体音色。专辑以器乐为主，横跨比利时民间与世界音乐传统，涵盖罗姆音阶、手风琴bal-musette、巴洛克室内乐、阿拉伯与地中海融合等风格。从Rómeó Bikar的泛欧罗姆小提琴，到Charlotte Pelgen的Django风格爵士摇摆，再到Amber Haddad的乌德琴阿拉伯风作品，以及Andries Boone的巴洛克曼陀林与羽管键琴组合，每位音乐家都以各自传统回应修道院的氛围。专辑历时三年制作，录音师巧妙利用古石建筑的声学特性，整体呈现出多元文化在统一空间中交织的宁静感。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张由瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威音乐家组成的室内三重奏专辑，以非传统方式重新诠释斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材。评论指出，作品虽以舞曲旋律为来源，但呈现方式更接近室内乐——三位乐手沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，试图挖掘旋律中隐含的深层意义与暗流。专辑以挪威塞特斯达尔地区的小提琴曲《Fossgrimen》开篇，借瀑布精灵传说暗示音乐中潜在的邪恶与神秘底色。演奏中可见乐器跨界配置：竖笛、萨克管、风笛与打击乐并置，传统与现代语汇交织。评论以《Polska from Per Myhr》为例，说明旋律在演奏中逐渐瓦解、断裂，最终归于静止。这种碎片化的处理方式赋予传统素材新的张力与反思空间。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一场两小时的无脚本独奏即兴录音，后经后期制作叠加人声采样、打击乐、音循环、田野录音和环境音效，孕育出这张充满冥想气质的专辑。评论详细呈现了 Sosa 的创作哲学：他拒绝被任何风格标签定义，从爵士、拉丁、廷巴、雷鬼到古典均有所涉猎却又刻意回避，强调'少即是多'与第一遍即兴的原始真实性。专辑融合了爵士即兴、世界音乐元素与实验性声音处理，Fazioli 三角钢琴的丰富共鸣被充分挖掘，呼应了'人类精神需要进化但也要保留传统'的创作理念。作品以沉稳的节奏探索声音质感，展现出深厚的艺术底蕴与持续进化的创造力。

items._cn_summary: Phill Niblock 的作品将原声乐器视为素材来源而非表达终点，通过大量叠加音轨与微音差冲突，使最终的声响结果有时完全遮蔽了原始乐器的音色。评论指出，即便是低音单簧管这样具有鲜明音色的乐器，也难以被这种极端的多轨叠加手法完全隐没。该专辑延续了 Niblock 标志性的密集泛音织体与极简主义声响美学，将单一乐器推至声学极限。Sub Rosa 厂牌的发行背景契合其地下实验音乐的定位。然而原文篇幅极短，仅为评论开篇片段，无法深入了解作品的具体结构、创作背景及艺术成就，信息量不足以支撑更高评价。

items.body: Francis Buseko considers the exquisite balance created by the post-White Hotel Salfordian Duo who create a sense of yearning for the sensation of yearning CURSED FRAME [DELUXE EDITION] by ANOTHER COUNTRY $$$$ Another day. Another ghost. Another shadow. Another thought. Another possibility. Another door. Another doorway behind the door. “Another” is a fitting word attached to a record that rarely stays where you expect it to. Cursed Frame is an album full of thresholds: sounds coming from across the room, voices emerging from the fog, something moving beneath the surface. Just when you think you have found your bearings, the music shifts the ground beneath you. There is always another layer, another shadow, another doorway behind the one you have just walked... items._cn_summary: Another Country $$$$ 来自英国索尔福德，被视为后白酒店（post-White Hotel）流派分支，作品以迷幻氛围与实验声响著称。《Cursed Frame》（豪华再版）是一张充满门槛感的专辑：声音从房间另一端传来，人声自雾气中浮现，表面之下始终有某种东西在移动。评论者使用「another」一词反复呼应专辑的不稳定性——音乐总是在听众以为已找到方位时再度移位，层层叠叠的声响构造出对「渴望」这种感受本身的渴望。这种文本-声音交织的暧昧美学与白酒店厂牌（White Hotel）的现场艺术传统一脉相承，注重氛围营造与听觉空间的多义性，适合偏好氛围实验与跨类型融合的听众。但评论正文内容偏短，所能获取的创作细节有限。

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — The World of Genius Hans is an excellent example of the more jazz-oriented, experimental and eccentric side of early-70s progressive rock. The second album by the French band Moving Gelatine Plates, it dives deeply into the Canterbury Scene, combining progressive rock, jazz-rock, psychedelia and a good dose of satirical humor.What stands out the most is the complexity of the compositions. The songs seem carefully constructed, especially in their instrumental sections, featuring several rhythmic changes, thematic development and interesting interactions between the instruments. Despite this complexity, the changes generally feel natural and do not seem to exist merely to show off technical skills.The instrumentation is probably one of the album's greatest strengths. Guitars, bass, drums, keyboards, saxophones, flute and other instruments create a very rich sound. The musicians demonstrate good technical ability, but fortunately the virtuosity remains subordinate to the compositions. The result is a technically sophisticated album without becoming excessively cold or purely focused on instrumental showmanship.The influence of the Canterbury Scene is quite evident, especially from bands such as Caravan and Soft Machine. Some elements also recall the more eclectic and experimental side of progressive rock. Nevertheless, Moving Gelatine Plates manages to develop a personality of its own, particularly through its humor, unusual instrumentation and combination of jazz and progressive rock structures.The title track, "The World of Genius Hans," is the main highlight. At around 14 minutes, it features numerous rhythmic changes, strong jazz influences and interesting synthesizer passages. It summarizes the album's overall concept very well and demonstrates the band's ability to work with long compositions without abandoning melodic ideas."Funny Doll" and "Astromonster" are also among the best moments of the album. The former presents a very characteristic approach from the band, while "Astromonster" explores a more psychedelic and experimental atmosphere.Another positive aspect is the album's cohesion. Despite the variety of ideas and styles, the album works very well as a complete listening experience. There is a relatively consistent musical identity throughout the record, and the alternation between more intense, jazzy, psychedelic and humorous moments keeps the listener interested.The production also deserves praise. Even though this is an early-70s recording, the instruments are relatively easy to distinguish, allowing the listener to appreciate the details of the complex arrangements.I would not consider the album perfect. Although the compositions are very interesting, a few passages can feel somewhat random, and the influence of other Canterbury Scene bands is quite noticeable. Therefore, despite its quality and complexity, I would not place it among the absolutely essential progressive rock albums.Nevertheless, The World of Genius Hans is highly recommended for fans of the Canterbury Scene, jazz-rock and the more experimental sides of progressive rock. It should also appeal to jazz-fusion fans who are interested in exploring progressive rock.Best tracks:1. The World of Genius Hans2. Funny Doll3. AstromonsterHonorable mention: Les �tres d'Or (bonus track)A highly recommended album for fans of Canterbury Scene, jazz-rock and progressive rock, particularly for listeners who enjoy complex arrangements, unusual instrumentation, frequent rhythmic changes and a humorous experimental approach.
items._genre: Canterbury Scene / jazz-rock / progressive rock / psychedelic
items._cn_summary: 这张1972年的专辑是法国乐队Moving Gelatine Plates的第二张作品，深入探索坎特伯雷流派，融合前卫摇滚、爵士摇滚与迷幻元素，并以讽刺幽默贯穿始终。评论指出，专辑最突出的特点在于编曲的复杂性，乐章经过精心构建，器乐段落包含丰富的节奏变化与主题发展，但这些变化大多自然流畅，并非单纯炫技。乐器编制相当丰富，涵盖吉他、贝斯、鼓、键盘、萨克斯与长笛等，形成层次饱满的织体，技术能力服务于整体结构。同名长篇作品《The World of Genius Hans》以十四分钟的篇幅集中呈现了乐队的核心理念——丰富的节奏切换、强烈的爵士影响与合成器段落的有机融合。《Funny Doll》与《Astromonster》分别展现了乐队的标志性手法与迷幻实验氛围。整体而言，专辑具备较强的内在统一性，各曲风格虽有变化却保持了清晰的音乐身份，录音制作也较为清晰。不过评论也指出，作品在某些段落略显随意，且受坎特伯雷其他乐队影响明显，未达到不可或缺的地位。

items._cn_summary: 本文为关于英国制作人Ken Thomas职业生涯的概述型报告，涵盖其1970年代末至2021年逝世期间在独立音乐领域的制作活动。重点阐述其如何将工业音乐的粗粝能量与后摇、梦幻流行的氛围质感相融合，以及在录音棚中发展的独特录音方法论。文中提及Wire、Psychic TV、Sigur Rós、M83等乐队，分析了从Trident Studios到冰岛改造泳池录音棚的工作方式演变。整体为人物综述性质的文本，缺乏对具体音乐作品的深度听觉分析。

The post Don’t Resolve the Dissonance: Meakusma Festival 2026 appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评来自 The Quietus，聚焦比利时德语区 Eupen 举办的 Meakusma 音乐节现场报道。文章以生动笔触描绘了实验音乐现场的混乱与张力：一位名叫 Saba Arat 的表演者在狭小空间内将话筒像套索一样甩过头顶，第一支话筒已撞墙碎裂，围观者纷纷举手护脸后退。作者 Robert Barry 以这种近乎暴力的现场行为切入，暗示 Meakusma 音乐节作为欧洲实验音乐重镇所呈现的丰富声景——从自由即兴到噪音、电子、声音艺术的多元交汇。文中未深入评论具体音乐技术细节，而是通过身体性的现场观察传递节日的实验氛围与不可预测性。Meakusma 历来以电子音乐与声音艺术为核心，融合即兴、噪音与装置表演，是比利时小众实验音乐生态的重要平台。

items.body: Review by JavierMiranda — Datura Lodge have arrived with something that feels fully formed, confident, and genuinely exciting to listen to, the kind of record that makes you want to tell people about it.The album opens with three tracks, "Mummy", "Stone" and "98 and 94", that flow into each other without a break, and that decision alone tells you a lot about how this band thinks. It works brilliantly. By the time the suite ends you are already hooked, pulled in by the atmosphere and the melodic instinct that runs through everything they do. The arrangements are detailed and rich, with Adam Holzman on keyboards and Ben Karas adding an electrifying violin solo on "Stone", but the melodies are always front and centre, and they stick."Hole" is worth stopping on for a moment. It has that slow-build quality that the best prog tracks share, a patient emotional arc that keeps growing until the guitar solo arrives and just says everything the words could not. There is a Pink Floyd shadow over it that feels completely natural rather than imitated.And then there is "Lodge", which closes the album and is, for me, the best thing on it. It starts with a quiet acoustic passage that immediately brings Genesis to mind, not in an obvious way, just that same sense of stillness and intention. From there it builds into something bigger and more modern, but without ever losing the melodic thread. It is a really moving piece of music.I have played this album a lot and it keeps giving. One of the best progressive rock records of the year. Five stars.
items._genre: heavy prog / progressive rock / symphonic rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以三首连奏开篇构成无间断组曲，键盘与小提琴独奏交织出层次丰富的编曲，旋律始终居于核心位置。《Hole》以渐进式情绪弧线展开，吉他独奏替代文字完成表达，整体带有Pink Floyd式空间感却不流于模仿。终曲《Lodge》以原声段落起始，氛围宁静而克制，随后逐步铺展为更宏大的现代声响。作为重型前卫摇滚作品，其制作成熟、器乐配置完整，偏向经典流派传承而非实验突破，与用户偏好的实验前卫、爵士即兴、电子暗潮等方向存在一定距离，但在旋律编织与情绪推进方面展现出扎实的创作功底。

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 986Brand X is a British progressive rock band that was founded in London in 1975. Brand X was a jazz fusion band that was active between 1975 and 1980 and had a hiatus from 1980 to 1992. The band was disbanded in 1999 and was reformed in 2016. Brand X is one of the best, most original and well known British bands in the 70's of the jazz/rock fusion scene. Phil Collins formed Brand X in 1975, with Percy Jones, John Goodsall and Robin Lumley. The debut studio album of Brand X, "Unorthodox Behavior" that was released in 1976, presented a band more rooted in the jazz wave than in rock. From that moment, Brand X became an autonomous group, performing live with Preston Heyman on drums instead of Collins, due to his duties with Genesis, although he continued to record with them. Their second studio album, "Moroccan Roll" released in the following year, featured a fifth member, Morris Pert, in addition to Phil.So, "Moroccan Roll" is the second studio album of Brand X that was released in 1977. The line up on "Moroccan Roll" is composed by John Goodsall (backing vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, sitar and effects), Robin Lumley (backing vocals, piano, Fender Rhodes electric piano, autoharp, clavinet, Minimoog ARP Odyssey synthesizer, Roland String synthesizer and effects), Percy Jones (bass, autoharp, marimba and effects), Phil Collins (lead vocals, drums, piano and effects) and Morris Pert (percussion).With their second album, Brand X continued to develop the sound of their debut work "Unorthodox Behaviour". Many of the most familiar elements are still there, like light footed evocative jazz rock with dense textures. However, some new ingredients are also thrown into the mix. As the title itself suggests, the album features, in addition to the jazz rock mix found on their debut album, research and experiments with sounds from the Middle and Far East, mainly from countries like Morocco. So, "Moroccan Roll" delivers a competent jazz rock with small doses of oriental sounds that never make the album boring or tiring. Commercially, the band fared better with this one than with their debut, albeit to a modest extent. Overall, this is an album rated well by the critics and was very well received by the fans of the band."Sun In The Night" is a laid back music, the only one on the album that has words. It sounds neither like Morocco nor like more rock'n'roll. The intensity grows as the song progresses. This is a peculiar, but yet fascinating piece of music. The next two tracks "Why Should I Lend You Mine..." and "...Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" move in a completely different direction musically. "Why Should I Lend You Mine" is an excellent instrumental full of surprises ranging from its varied dynamics to the curious percussion and the always virtuous and extended sound of Jones's fretless. Lumley and Goodsall's solos move within an environment where everything seems to levitate. "Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" is a brief piece that could well be the coda of the previous one. "Hate Zone" and "Collapsar" complete the A side of the LP. A solo by Collins kicks "Hate Zone" for several seconds. Jones then joins in on the euphoric piece, followed by the rest of the band. This is a very hard grooving track that clearly moves towards jazz rock. The short and spacey "Collapsar" is full of various Lumley's keyboard sounds and takes us down that levitating path for a minute and a half. "Disco Suicide" is an excellent piece, one of the best built on the album. The track is divided into faster and calmer parts that sound a bit different every time they are repeated. Brand X has added vocals for the final segment of this composition. The very short "Orbits" demonstrates the instrumental mastery of Jones with his unparalleled flair and technique. The only instrument on this track is the bass and various effects. The jam session character of "Malaga Virgin" makes this track come closest to the material from "Unorthodox Behaviour". The piece switches between the fast and slow, loud and quiet parts. The interplay is exceedingly virtuosic, especially the solo segments by Jones and Lumley. "Macrocosm" is a celebration of the fusion genre, being intricate and uplifting, a showcase for the individual skills of the musicians. It shows why Brand X has been one of the jazz fusion bands with great relevance for decades.Conclusion: "Moroccan Roll", unlike its predecessor, credits the tracks to individual authors. So, obviously, it's not as jam session based as their debut album. It contains some very interesting musical ideas. The Far East sounds play a very important role. The band presents nine tracks, all of which are fascinating in their own way. From wonderfully calm songs to fascinatingly restless jazz fusion songs with progressive parts, everything is represented with the highest quality. This album ended up being the farewell of Collins, who had to leave since he accumulated the post of vocalist and drummer of Genesis. For those who want to hear developed music with emotion this record definitely offers this perfectly, but if you want the true spirit of Brand X and jazz fusion "Unorthodox Behaviour" is for sure the album to get.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)
items._genre: jazz rock / fusion / world fusion / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 这是英国融合乐队Brand X的第二张录音室专辑，延续了首张作品的轻盈爵士摇滚质感，同时引入中东和远东声音元素，尤其是摩洛哥风格的实验探索。专辑编制丰富，吉他、键盘、贝斯、鼓与打击乐各展其能，John Goodsall演奏电吉他、原声吉他与西塔琴，Robin Lumley负责多种键盘与合成器，Percy Jones的无品贝斯线条充满延伸性与张力，Phil Collins与Morris Pert共同构成双鼓/打击乐配置。曲目方面，唯一的 vocal 曲目《Sun In The Night》氛围松弛，强度随推进逐渐提升；《Why Should I Lend You Mine...》动态多变，打击乐与无品贝斯即兴交织，键盘与吉他独奏在悬浮感的声场中展开。整体上，这是一张融合了爵士摇滚骨架与世界音乐调料的作品，兼顾技术性与氛围感。

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular flatness to Milanese light through the cold months, an industrial grey that tends to reduce ambition to habit and every gesture to the merely reasonable. It is not, on its face, a light out of which cathedrals of sound get built from vibraphone and French horn, harp and string quartet folded into the frame of a rock band. And yet in that grey and reasonable city, at the turn between 1972 and 1973, three young musicians decided otherwise.Alberto Ravasini, Roberto Giuliani and Sandro Lorenzetti formed the first nucleus, carrying between them the vocabulary of jazz clubs and rehearsal rooms rather than concert halls. By the middle of 1973 they had doubled in size, joined by Sergio Lattuada, Maurizio Bianchini and Leonardo Schiavone, whose training had run through classical counterpoint rather than blues scales. The new sextet took the name Maxophone, a word that reads, not unreasonably, as a cousin of saxophone and megaphone, and set about proving that a band built from two opposing musical educations need not choose between them.It took until 1975 for that proof to reach record shops, by which point the golden years of Rock Progressivo Italiano, the years of Le Orme's Uomo Di Pezza and Banco's first two albums, already lay a season or two behind. Sandro Colombini, the producer behind much of Banco del Mutuo Soccorso's early success and many other credits across the decade, brought Maxophone to Produttori Associati, a label built on film scores and jazz sessions that rarely strayed into rock at all. The album was recorded across February, March and April of that year at the Ricordi studios in Milan, engineered by Gaetano Ria, and preceded into the world by a single pairing its opening and third tracks.The cover fell to Cesare Monti, working as always alongside Wanda Monti, the same hand that two years earlier had assembled the notorious collage for Museo Rosenbach's Zarathustra. Where that image courted scandal, this one is content with mystery, and the record inside asks for nothing but attention.What Maxophone built across six songs and forty minutes borrows from everywhere without settling anywhere for long. There is the choral warmth of Genesis in the vocal writing, the keyboard muscle of Emerson in Lattuada's organ runs, the wind instrument menace of King Crimson circa Lizard in Bianchini's horn and Schiavone's reeds, a jazz vocabulary that never announces itself as foreign to the material, and underneath all of it a folk undertow that keeps the whole apparatus rooted in something recognisably Italian. Harp, violin, cello and double bass arrive as guests rather than ornaments, thickening the sextet into something closer to a small orchestra without ever slowing its reflexes.- C'� Un Paese Al Mondo: a piano figure opens onto an imagined country built on ideals of fairness and unclouded truth, sung with a conviction that makes utopia sound briefly plausible, before clarinet, trumpet and a hardening guitar drag the song back toward the actual world.- Fase: the only instrumental here, and the boldest proof of what six formally trained ears can do together, guitar and saxophone trading a nervous energy that resolves, unexpectedly, into forty seconds of vibraphone stillness before the current picks back up.- Al Mancato Compleanno Di Una Farfalla: a classical guitar figure and a flute line that could have wandered in from early Jethro Tull, framing a lyric that hands a fading butterfly's colours forward to whoever comes next, tender where the album's other songs tend toward argument.- Elzeviro: church organ and a voice alone at first, then the leaden weight of the mid seventies pressing in, the image of a man outnumbered and a power already convulsing as it comes apart, before the band answers with one of the record's most searing guitar solos.- Mercanti Di Pazzie: harp and a borrowed phrase from Hindemith's sonata open onto the album's most fragile interior, a dream logic that trades argument for atmosphere and asks to be believed rather than followed.- Antiche Conclusioni Negre: horns and drums in full voice from the first bar, a nine minute survey of everything the band knows how to do, closing on a low choir over solo organ that sounds less like an ending than a valediction.An English sung version followed the same year, with new lyrics credited to a certain J. Bratel rather than straight translations, carrying different titles and a reshuffled running order. It found little of an audience abroad, and history has settled comfortably on the Italian original as the version worth defending.By 1977 the band had time for one more single, Il Fischio Del Vapore backed with Cono Di Gelato, gentler and more modest than anything on the album, and then Maxophone simply stopped. Produttori Associati's brief and uncharacteristic venture into rock had not paid off, the wider scene it belonged to was already contracting around it, and six musicians who had spent years learning to think as one orchestra went back to thinking separately. Schiavone drifted briefly through Stormy Six before settling with the pop group Accademia. All six had already lent their hands, uncredited on the album sleeve but present on tape, to Corrado Castellari's Gente Cos� that same year.It might have ended there, one record and a rumour passed between collectors, had Sergio Lattuada not spent the following decades unwilling to let it. A 2005 box set gathered the unreleased sessions under a title, From Cocoon To Butterfly, that borrowed its own imagery from a five minute song about a fading insect. Three years later Lattuada and Ravasini rebuilt the group around new players, carried it as far as a stage in Tokyo, and in 2017 released a second album carrying words the poet Roberto Roversi had written for them before his own death in 2012. The story closed for good in May of 2018, when Lattuada died and took with him the will that had kept the chrysalis open.What survives on tape from 1975 does not need that later history to justify itself, but it colours the listening all the same. Six players who might easily have spent their careers as session musicians for other people's songs chose instead to spend one album proving what happens when every instrument in the room gets a vote. The sheer plenty of ideas occasionally denies the songs the settled inevitability of the genre's very greatest single statements, and that, rather than any failure of craft or feeling, is the only real argument against calling this an unqualified masterpiece. Everything else argues the other way. Among the crowded company of Italian progressive rock's one album wonders, Maxophone stands close to the summit, and deserves to be met there. My rating: 4,5/5(Bassano del Grappa, Italy, September 2026)
items._genre: rock progressivo italiano / jazz-rock / chamber prog
items._cn_summary: 这张1975年的意大利前卫摇滚专辑由六人乐队Maxophone录制于米兰Ricordi录音室，融合了爵士俱乐部语汇与古典对位训练两种截然不同的音乐教育背景。乐队在键盘、风乐器（圆号、单簧管、巴松管）与摇滚框架之间搭建桥梁，同时引入竖琴、小提琴、大提琴和低音提琴作为客座乐器，使六重奏呈现出小型管弦乐队的质感。歌词探讨理想国与公平真理的命题，配合Genesis式的合唱温暖感、Emerson式的键盘力度以及King Crimson式的管乐威胁感，根部则维系着一层意大利民谣的暗流。专辑封面由曾为Museo Rosenbach设计封面的Monti夫妇操持，以神秘取代丑闻。整体制作在Produttori Associati厂牌完成，录音工程师为Gaetano Ria，母带呈现六首歌四十分钟的篇幅。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — William D. Drake's solo debut was like reshuffling the deck and starting almost from scratch, though in his case, it is a very special kind of "zero," one rich with nuances that allow for a variety of elements foreign to the Cardiacs' universe to enter the mix. It is a collection of seventeen songs, best described, were it a speech, as "logorrheic", that unfold like tales of life in nature, rural history, mysticism, mythology, and the presence of forests or the sea in English folklore (as heard in the track "The Great Adventurer"). It is no surprise, then, to find Baroque and chamber music accompanying a rock style that is highly artistic yet secular, at once cinematic, psychedelic, and dissonant. From the opening piano notes of "Miaow Miaow," we are instantly transported to another time and place; "Sky in yer Lap" feels like something out of a Shakespearean production, while "Love in an Overcoat" evokes the atmosphere of a cabaret. Throughout the album, the harmonium establishes an antique spirit, one that, in its very antiquity, becomes modern.The track "Paradox" reminded me of John Cale and his piano, evoking something visceral, raw, and stark, though Drake adds repetitive backing vocals that drive the dark, Victorian atmosphere to a fever pitch. There is something hypnotic about "Poor John"; its polyrhythms and trumpet evoke an end-of-the-world orchestra in a medieval city under siege by the plague. Yet, rest assured, "Dragonfly" pulls us away from that scene, transporting us instead to a silent movie screening."Ivy Dun" possesses a level of absurdity...of madness...that makes it one of my favorites; few pieces of music have the power to be so immediate, so direct, it strikes like an invisible bolt of lightning. That chorus and percussion, combined with the piano, don't ask for permission; they simply take hold and keep on reverberating."Lists of Clay," with its organ and deep vocals, is Peter Hammill on The Future Now; it is Gog Magog on In Camera; it is everything right in this upside-down world."Fiery Pyre," with its Eastern flair, reminded me of Siouxsie & The Banshees, while the piano and vocals could easily have been David Bowie; the album is full of nuances, secrets, and hidden compartments waiting to be discovered, each time revealing something new. It is like a labyrinth one never fully masters, despite always being in the same place.Perhaps the place itself is an illusion, a thought that arises while listening to "The Perfect Crime," a track that feels like something straight out of a 1970s Brian Eno record.And it all comes together, Cardiacs, their spirit, and an English past brought into the present with "Quivvy Vivvy." Here, a vaudeville-style format featuring multiple short songs proves the perfect vehicle to convey "Freedom and Love", fittingly, the final, deeply moving track of an ideal debut album, paving the way for several more yet to be discovered.
items._genre: eclectic prog / chamber pop / baroque / psychedelic rock / avant-folk
items._cn_summary: William D. Drake首张个人专辑收录十七首曲目，将巴洛克与室内乐元素注入摇滚框架，形成兼具艺术性与世俗感的折衷风格。整体音乐语言多变：开场钢琴引入复古氛围，手风琴贯穿全篇营造古旧质感；部分曲目运用多节奏与铜管制造末世感，另一些则带有维多利亚时期的暗黑戏剧张力。专辑涉及自然、乡村历史、神秘主义、神话及英式民间传说等主题，歌词密集，叙事性强。编曲上融合卡巴莱、默片配乐、东方色彩与民谣元素，钢琴、管风琴与打击乐的组合富层次感。整张作品拒绝单一风格标签，每首曲目都像独立的场景或短篇，具有探索性与实验倾向，适合喜欢跨界融合与文学性歌词的听众。

items.body: Margate, Kent-based musician Tim Horne has released “An Ocean Apart”, the first single from his new album “Transmutation”, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts. Horne composes cinematic ambient and electronic music using synthesisers, acoustic instruments and field recordings. “An Ocean Apart” comes with a video by @diz_qo, built around artwork by Mariz Nigro, and the single is also available on Spotify and Apple Music. Horne describes “An Ocean Apart” as the emotional core of the album. “It forms the emotional core of the album and is imbued with paradoxical feelings of distance and closeness, isolation and connection. These are contradictory emotions I’ve oscillated between when looking back with unreliable memory and nostalgia,” he said. Tim Horne’s ‘Transmutation’ due October 8 “Transmutation” runs eight tracks: “Requiem,” “Halcyon,” “Biota,” “An Ocean Apart,” “Volta,” “Folie à Deux,” “Ascension” and “Metamorphosis.” Horne wrote, performed and produced every track himself, with additional mixing and mastering by Thomas Farmer and artwork by Mariz Nigro. The album was recorded towards the end of a long-term relationship and works through contradictory memories of joy and sorrow alongside an embrace of change. Horne layers flute and other acoustic instruments with analog, digital and modular synthesizers, often processing them until they no longer resemble their source material. He has pointed to Wendy Carlos, Kraftwerk, Boards of Canada, Sigur Rós, M83, Radiohead, Nils Frahm, Alessandro Cortini, R Beny, Emily Sprague, Ann Annie, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Jogging House and Hainbach as influences on the record. Transmutation by Tim Horne “Transmutation” is available to pre-order now as a digital album and as a limited-edition CD in a card wallet, both through Bandcamp, with the full record following on release day. About Tim Horne Tim Horne is a musician based in Margate, Kent. He spent roughly a decade playing bass, synthesisers and backing vocals in bands including Linear Loveboxx, Inca Maps and Inigo Blue & The System before moving into solo work. He self-released two solo albums built from modular-synthesizer improvisation, “Rise” (2022) and “Clusters” (2023). Horne developed his current sound over two years through the regular live sessions hosted by Coastal Electronauts, a collective of electronic and experimental artists based in nearby Whitstable, and that process led to the eight tracks on “Transmutation.” The album, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts, follows those two solo releases and is preceded by the single “An Ocean Apart.”
items._cn_summary: 这是英国肯特郡马尔盖特音乐人Tim Horne第三张个人专辑的首支单曲预告。专辑名为《Transmutation》，由小厂牌Coastal Electronauts于2026年10月发行，共八首曲目，全部由Horne独自创作、演奏并制作。Horne以模块合成器、模拟与数字合成器为核心，叠加长笛等原声乐器与田野录音，并对声音进行深度处理，使原始音源面目全非。这种做法将原声乐器的自然质感与电子合成器的抽象纹理融为一体。专辑创作于一段长期关系走向终结的时期，作品探讨回忆中的欢乐与悲伤等矛盾情绪。Horne的音乐渊源横跨古典电子（Wendy Carlos、Kraftwerk）、梦幻流行（Boards of Canada、M83、Radiohead）、当代古典氛围（Nils Frahm、R Beny、Emily Sprague）以及实验电子（Alessandro Cortini、Hainbach）等领域。整体定位介于氛围音乐与电影配乐之间，具备一定实验性与跨界融合意识，但偏向氛围叙事而非极端前卫手法。
