items.body: We speak of falling in love as though gravity should handle the labor. The harder truth is that affection asks for practice: the slow unlearning of fear, vanity, possession, and the reflex to flee when another person reaches the unguarded parts of us. To say “I learn to love” is to leave the verb unfinished. It admits that tenderness is no permanent achievement, but an education measured in repetition, failure, and the willingness to try again. Austin psych-goth trio The Schisms make that unfinished education move on “I Learn To Love,” the first single from their forthcoming four-track EP, Tejas, due October 2. The song’s unruly new video was created with Austin film crew Three-Eyed Cat Collective. Led by singer, songwriter, and guitarist Carson Barker, The Schisms also feature Goose McCollum on bass, keys, and vocals and Michael Stockton on drums and vocals. The track enters on a sustained guitar figure and a firm, forward-driving beat, while Barker’s voice glides over the groove with studied ease. A blues-bitten guitar answers him in metallic clanks; the cymbals then open the ceiling as his delivery rises from a low croon into a full-throated command. Thick proto-metal chords eventually press against the rhythm section, giving the song the physical force of a taproom floor under too many boots. Much of its frame belongs to late-’60s and early-’70s rock, but an ominous synth bed disrupts the period logic midway through. A buzzing keyboard figure leans toward prog, and Barker’s voice multiplies into an eerie, reverb-drenched cascade. The old forms are dragged into an unstable present. The riff walks into the room with its collar open, while the electronics quietly change the locks. Barker wrote “I Learn To Love” as a reach toward a higher state of mind, with much of the lyric arriving spontaneously the night before the recording session. The song continued to take shape on the fly with Grammy-winning producer and engineer Stuart Sikes, known for his work with The White Stripes, Cat Power, and Loretta Lynn. Early James Brown and Bo Diddley can be heard in its insistence on rhythm, although The Schisms route that bodily drive through punk abrasion, psychedelic color, and goth unease. A mantra found a backbeat and acquired teeth; The Schisms make self-improvement sound gloriously disreputable. That productive disorder carries into the video. The clip opens on the exposed conditions of the shoot, with Stockton playing against a bare green screen as studio lights and equipment remain plainly visible. Soon the band are swallowed by liquid blue forms, clipped into circular windows, outlined like cheap television ghosts, and deposited among Texas flags, cattle, cactus country, cowboy hats, fire, leather, and collapsing VHS interference. At points, the trio look as though they were keyed into a public-access broadcast seconds before the tape began to warp. By returning to the uncovered green screen at the end, the clip makes its fakery part of its regional portrait. Texas becomes birthright and prop, affectionate cliché and private joke. Austin appears less as a civic postcard than as a fever dream assembled after last call. “For the video, we wanted to do something really trashy, like an old Captain Beafheart vid mixed with VHS-style visual effects. We also wanted something that represents Austin from a born-and-raised Texan’s point of view. There is definitely a grittier, maniacal side of Austin subcultures that often gets overlooked in the media. We wanted to pair that with cliché Texas themes. There are some throwbacks to Nathan and I’s favorite filmmakers, like Jodorowsky. The song was half-written in the studio on the fly with Stuart Sikes. It just felt like a chaotic Bo Diddley song with a dash of punk and psych, so we went with it.” Watch the video for “I Learn To Love” below: Listen to The Schisms’ “I Learn To Love” via Spotify or Apple Music, and order the single through Bandcamp. I Learn To Love by The Schisms Tejas extends the single’s upward turn. Barker wrote half of the EP during a winter spent alone in a one-bedroom log cabin in the Colorado mountains and completed the remaining material in the studio with Sikes. Isolation gave him a practical brief: write the music capable of lifting his own spirits. The result steps away from some of the darker concerns of The Schisms’ previous album, Moon, in favor of something brighter, punchier, and more open to instinct. Barker initially wrote and recorded each instrumental part before bringing the songs to McCollum and Stockton for their input. The name Tejas draws on the word’s association with friendship, while the record itself is Texas-made from end to end. Barker, McCollum, Stockton, Sikes, and Barker’s brother, who created the artwork, are all native Texans. The three musicians grew up in the same town and knew one another for years, although differences in age and timing kept them from sharing a band until the current lineup came together. “The universe just threw us together, and it’s been amazingly positive,” Barker says. His search for McCollum began with an unusually exact request: “I’m looking for a leather daddy who plays a vintage Rickenbacker bass left-handed. Know anyone?” Stockton joined after letting Barker stay at his house for a month while Barker was between homes. “The chemistry is so positive,” Barker adds, “I feel like we’re the fucking Teletubbies.” Partially funded by the City of Austin Live Music Fund, Tejas arrives October 2, 2026. Tejas tracklist: I Learn To Love One Blood All the Good Things Beyond Death The Schisms begin a 15-date fall tour on September 11 at Houston’s Black Magic Social Club. From there, the band follows the Gulf Coast to New Orleans and Jackson before moving through Birmingham, Athens, and three North Carolina stops. Nashville and Memphis carry the run into its western return through Little Rock, Dallas, Oklahoma City, and Denton. The final date brings the band home to Austin on the day Tejas is released, turning The Far Out Lounge into the record’s natural point of arrival. Tour dates: September 11 — Houston, TX @ Black Magic Social Club September 12 — New Orleans, LA @ Holy Diver September 13 — Jackson, MS @ Urban Foxes September 15 — Birmingham, AL @ The Nick September 16 — Athens, GA @ Athentic Brewing September 17 — Durham, NC @ Rubies on 5 Points September 18 — Greenville, NC @ Benny Vincenzo’s Pizza September 19 — Asheville, NC @ The One Stop September 20 — Nashville, TN @ The Cobra September 22 — Memphis, TN @ Haven Haus September 23 — Little Rock, AR @ Pizza D’s September 24 — Dallas, TX @ Craft & Growler September 25 — Oklahoma City, OK @ The Grand Royale September 26 — Denton, TX @ Anderson’s Distillery October 2 — Austin, TX @ The Far Out Lounge Follow The Schisms: Website Bandcamp SoundCloud Spotify Apple Music Instagram Facebook TikTok YouTube The post Austin Psych-Goth Trio The Schisms Unleash a Leather Clad Texas Fever Dream in the Video for “I Learn To Love” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: The Schisms 的这首单曲将学习去爱的不确定性作为核心隐喻，歌词在录音前夜自发成形，与曾与白线条乐队合作的制作人 Stuart Sikes 共同完成。编曲以延音吉他与稳定鼓点开场，歌手嗓音从低吟攀升至高亢呼喊，原型金属和弦与鼓点形成物理张力。中段插入不祥合成器音床，嗡鸣键盘向前卫摇滚倾斜，人声分裂为混响回响的诡异层叠，将六七十年代摇滚框架拖入不稳定的当下。节奏根源可追溯至早期詹姆斯·布朗与波·迪德利，但被朋克磨蚀、迷幻色彩与哥特不安重新路由，使自我完善听起来放荡不羁。MV由奥斯汀电影团队制作，暴露的绿幕与演播室灯光成为视觉元素，乐队被蓝色液态形态吞噬，置于德州旗帜、仙人掌、牛仔帽与皮革图像中，VHS干扰效果贯穿始终，揭示影像虚构性本身。

items.body: Punk may have changed the musical landscape and proved that anyone with a guitar and a mission statement could start a band, but the years that followed expanded punk’s simplicity in countless exciting directions. Sometimes, it blows my mind just how many incredible bands and movements formed in the wake of the punk explosion. From 1976-1982 alone, the sheer amount of musical creativity is staggering, with so many bands quick to combine punk’s feral, DIY essence with art rock instrumentation; spacier, dubbed-out rhythms; bleak industrial textures; and much, much more. In the UK, hundreds of bands formed in the wake of the Sex Pistols, who begat Joy Division, The Banshees, and Cabaret Voltaire, who begat thousands of other bands that we all know and love today. One of the most lasting and beloved bands from the original UK post-punk boom was Sad Lovers & Giants. Formed in Watford in 1980 by Garce (Simon) Allard, guitarist Simon Blanchard, bassist Cliff Silver, drummer Nigel Pollard, and keyboardist/saxophonist David Wood, Sad Lovers & Giants (SLAG for short), quickly signed with Last Movement and Midnight Music and released a string of crucial early singles as a statement of intent. During those early years, the band was extremely prolific, cutting two moody full-length LPs in addition to these singles, each track as powerful as the last. The band caught the ear of John Peel and cultivated a devout cult following both on the strength of their studio recordings as well as their explosive live show. Soon after, the band would splinter, with Blanchard and Pollard leaving to form The Snake Corps. In 1987, SLAG would reform with a new lineup and release three incredible records that saw the band expanding their sound and influencing the budding dream pop movement. 1987’s The Mirror Test is a landmark album for me personally, and it’s impressive to hear the album’s lush textures reflected in countless bands today. Again, in 1991, the band went on hiatus, but have since returned in the new millennium and have rekindled the spark that brought them together all those years ago. Since reuniting in 2002 (and again in 2009 with Hicks), the band has performed hundreds of gigs (including their first series of shows in North America in 2016), recorded a session for LA’s Part Time Punks, released a handful of standalone singles, and recorded two full-length LPs. Their latest release, this year’s The Weight of Forgotten Dreams, features ten new tracks, all of which stay true to SLAG’s majestic sound and atmospheric energy. The album is currently available on CD, digital, and vinyl, and will be followed up by a highly anticipated documentary that aims to capture the band’s many evolutions and highlights over their 40+ year career. We had the chance to catch up with the current incarnation of SLAG, including vocalist/guitarist Garce Allard, original drummer Nigel Pollard, and current members Tony McGuinness, Will Hicks, and Ian Gibson, about the new album, the band’s legacy, and more. Former guitarist and close friend Simon Blanchard also drops in for a spell… Congratulations on the new album! Can you tell us a bit about the recording of it? Garce: Our writing and recording processes aren’t separate. We have home studios in which we produce demos that are saved into a SLAG Dropbox, there are files for demos, instrumentals and raw vocal and sax stems. If anyone comes up with a demo it goes in the appropriate file. I always save a AIFF of my raw vocals at every stage. Usually what happens next is that the demos are played at rehearsal and everybody contributes ideas. Quite often these ideas are road tested at live shows and subtle changes are made, then it’s back to the original demo which gets an upgrade. When the demo file and instrumental file look like they are full enough to consider an album we produce a provisional running order and work out what needs doing to each track before it can be handed over to Igor and Tony to mix. Effectively, all the recording is done at home. The only time we go into a recording studio is if I need to ‘perform’ my vocals as we often notice they are different when I sing them in front of other people. This didn’t happen with the new record, so every vocal was recorded in the studio at the bottom of my garden. On a personal note, I write all the lyrics and whilst the others freely critique them I mainly use Nigel as a specific sounding board while a song develops, but Tony ultimately produces my vocals from the raw stems that I have comp’d and uploaded to the Dropbox file. Tony is the only person on the planet I would trust to edit the actual words I write as happened with a song on The Weight of Forgotten Dreams where I just got lost in thickets of words which needed a sympathetic pruning! Very occasionally we look in the demo files and there’s a long forgotten piece of music that is 95% album ready. This actually happened on this record. It’s been eight years between Mission Creep and The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams – were you working on the record all this time, or were you focused on other things? Garce: Song writing is a perpetual thing but the other project we’ve worked on over the last three years is the SLAG documentary being produced by Jean Paul Van Mierlo who did the excellent Adrian Borland film Walking in the Opposite Direction. This is with the same film maker Marc Waltman. This is your second record working with Igor Garanin – can you share some stories about working together? Garce: Igor is a mix engineer Tony knows through Above & Beyond and he did such a great job on Mission Creep that we used him again on the new album. Tony works with Igor in the studio and then sends us mixes for comment. How has your songwriting style evolved over the years? Garce: If you mean the way we get to a finished album, then the human process is very similar but the technology available now means we don’t have to do the traditional ‘recording studio’ thing. In that sense, we are effectively self-producing, whereas before, the person paying for the studio, i.e., Nick Ralph if it was Midnight Music, had a large say in the overall production decisions and the ‘style’ of the finished songs. But I think what you mean is the evolution of our style of song. Many other people will have many differing views on this and which album they like best and I accept it has changed subtly from album to album. Not a lot has changed vocally other than I’ve got better at writing melodies and perhaps more focused on saying what I want, in the way I want, in order to compliment the music and bring out the best in a song. Changes in personnel obviously bring an element of change so the key personnel swap was Tony McGuinness for Simon Blanchard on guitar after the second album. I could write an essay on that. Then there was Juliet Sainsbury (currently lives in LA) on keyboards in the eighties, she was the most accomplished keyboardist we’ve had so what she plays the others wouldn’t have been able to. Then we’ve had Cliff Silver on bass replaced by Ian Gibson and both are like chalk and cheese as musicians and songwriters. The net result of all this in my opinion, is that if anything the cinematic quality of the ambient strings and ‘wet’ noise has become more lush and expansive but…to a listener coming to the band now, the songs on the latest album have all the same sonic qualities and idiosyncrasies as all the other albums. We have a distinctive SLAG sound which we understand and respect. Nigel: Our style has not really changed over the years; we all know what makes a good SLAG song . Our songs stand the test of time, and I personally cannot distinguish between songs written 40 years ago to those that are on our latest album. Garce has and continues to write very emotional and evocative lyrics which many fans can connect with. Can you expand on some of the lyrics or themes behind the record? Garce: “We will be ashes, we will be silent and old, we will be wisdom, we will be left in the cold” were the lyrics I wrote as a twenty four year old for our second single “Things We Never Did.” I am now far older than the age I envisaged in that song and I have no intention of being silent or of being left in the cold! Broadly, I would describe my lyrics as ‘English Melancholia’ but I noticed a wry-ness creeping in over the course of this recent album, although given that I am writing about the state of the world as I currently see it there’s precious little to chuckle about; call it gallows humour. As a device, I often write against a fictional dystopian backdrop (“Asylum Town,” “Repentance Day,” “Down To The Wire”), but increasingly the dystopia has become reality since the last album in 2018. Unfortunately, that does seem to be the case, doesn’t it? Sad to think that all the prophecies, whether it be in lyrics or films or literature has come true, in a sense. On a lighter, but related note, what else, other than music, do you tend to draw inspiration from? Garce: Literature and Art Nigel: Differing cultures and the great outdoors. Sad Lovers & Giants have always had such iconic artwork across both your singles and LPs. The covers alone really convey such a strong sense of emotion and perfectly reflect the music in my opinion. I’d love to hear more about what inspires your album artwork. Garce: Simon Blanchard designed the sleeves for the first three singles, including the image for “Lost In a Moment” (girl in armchair with teddy bear!), which is one that is particularly well known. Given that he also wrote much of the songs I think his design choices were intuitively in alignment with his songwriting. Midnight Music did the design work for many subsequent releases but they were building on the foundations he had laid. We asked Simon to design The Weight of Forgotten Dreams as he did such a great job with the previous album, Mission Creep and Cherry Red Records asked him to design the box set they released. Simon: Well it’s imortant to remember I can’t claim credit for all the band’s sleevework and Tony’s contribution is not to be underestimated. It’s not always easy to provide a visual foil for their music, but having been there since the beginning, I probably have a basic understanding of the strange world they inhabit. There’s usually a lot of trial and error and this time it was helpful to have access to some of Garce’s original paintings, which I montaged-up with the photography. To me it felt that the result sat well with the music and luckily the band liked it. Will you be touring for this record? Garce: In SLAG world there are three things happening currently. The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams, the film and then the live double album recorded for the film, so we will be playing live more over the next two years to coincide with this creative phase. I was happy to hear that the band finally came to the US after all these years, but sadly I live in New York and couldn’t make it to the West Coast/Austin shows. Do you plan to come back to North America at all? Garce: We want to come back and at some point over this next two years would be great timing but we are not in any specific discussions at present. Obviously as we did the West Coast plus Canada and SXSW in Austin last time, the East Coast and New York would be a priority next time. In the Breeze-era lineup. Photo by Cliff Ash. Looking back to the formation of the band, can you tell us a bit about how you all came together? Garce: The band was originally formed by Simon, Nigel and Dave Wood, who were at school together. They were called The Traumatics and they recruited an outside bass player called Steve Carter who sadly died quite recently. Dave played tenor sax and both Simon and Steve sang. At that time I was playing guitar (and singing backing vocals) in another local band called Suspect Device and we knew each other from playing together supporting a well known local band called Mr E and The Imaginations. Mr E had supported The Ruts at The Marquee club and the guitarist and singer of The Ruts were at our gig. I knew Dave Wood from drinking and playing pool together at The Feathers in Rickmansworth and he invited me to audition as the singer of The Traumatics. From that first meeting we knew it would work because we shared the same musical tastes. Our first London gigs were performed as The Traumatics with Steve Carter on bass. When we did “50:50” he sang it and I played keyboards. We changed the name from The Traumatics to Sad Lovers & Giants in January 1981. Sometime after the first single we brought in Cliff Silver on bass who we knew from playing with other Watford bands that he was in. We also bought a string synth and Simon began experimenting with spacial guitar sounds. Dave began playing the string synth more than the sax. Simon: We formed pretty soon after the punk explosion in the late seventies. We had been listening to rock music for years before that as young teenagers but it suddenly became very clear that you could be in a band with only very rudimentary music skills. We slowly got better – but not that much. The Traumatics. Photo credit unknown. Mid-80s lineup. Photo by Nick Ralph. Was there a coherent scene in Watford? Garce: There were a lot of young bands who all knew each other and played and drank in the same pubs. There was the Watford Pub Rock competition run by the owner of the local music shop and there were several fanzines. Apart from ‘our sort of music’ i.e. Post Punk/New Wave/Alternative/Art School bands, there were other more mainstream rock and blues bands mainly comprised of older musicians. Watford was a seething mass of music and musicians but probably no different to many large towns in the early eighties. The UK music scene at that time was quite remarkable looking back on it. I listened to a BBC radio 4 programme the other day whose basic premise was that the counterculture of the ’60s didn’t die out but was boosted by punk and morphed into the indie scene of the ’80s. But then the establishment pushed back, Thatcherism (Margaret Thatcher, prime minister 1979 to 1990) was in effect a counter-counterculture where alternative views were discouraged. On the whole we weren’t overtly political but if you were in one of those young bands then you knew who the enemy was and just doing it was resistance of sorts. That was the true source of the apparent coherence. A disparate collection of bands from Watford and nearby towns got together and put out an album called The Thing From The Crypt but the DIY record scene was just a reflex in the instinctive resistance to the establishment. I love that compilation and was very happy to pick up the Dark Entries reissue a few years back! Otherwise, the band has such an iconic catalog of tracks, including bangers like “50:50,” “Seven Kinds of Sin,” “In Flux,” “Colourless Dream,” etc. that are still heard in clubs today. How do you feel about the band’s legacy thus far? Garce: When we started we were defining our sound and every new song we wrote was a step into the unknown. When we reformed in 2009 we were coming off the back of a reputation built over thirty years and eight albums so from then on there was a pressure to maintain the standards we had set. As a live band we’ve surpassed those early standards which comes not only from experience but from having a huge back catalogue of great songs to choose from; we have the songs and we know how to use them. These days we’ve scaled our live show up for some seriously large gigs and have sold out 1200 capacity venues in our own name but we are still a cult band albeit with a huge worldwide following. Sometimes I dream about suddenly becoming a mainstream act but in reality I’m quite happy being where we are. Which begs the question, “if it’s not about world domination what is it about?” Answer: the music, the fans, the international travel, the ‘pinch yourself’ moments when we achieve something surprising like having “Colourless Dream” used in the Netflix Andy Warhol series. But above all it’s about the shared experience of doing it all with your mates and…still being able to make music. As a post punk-eighties band, we are always going to be remembered for those first two albums but there are eight others and Spotify has helped get them heard with around 150,000 plays a month. I’m very proud of all of them; they are all unique and have their own story to tell. The trick with the last two has been to keep our essential ‘sound’ whilst conforming to modern production expectations because fans listen to the work recorded in the analogue world of the early eighties and the production standards of that era were completely different, nevertheless they are synonymous with what the fans think of as SLAG. That is acceptable when it’s tinged with nostalgia but not in the modern world. If I remember correctly there was hardly any compression used on the early albums, can you believe that? So I think The Weight of Forgotten Dreams sits well in the legacy scheme of things. But what next? Do we write one last happy album? Hopefully there will be many more to come! Can you share some personal highlights from over the years? Garce: Showcasing at SXSW in 2016 Nigel: Playing our first gig as Sad Lovers & Giants in our hometown of Rickmansworth, recording our second single (“Colourless Dream”) in Surrey Sound where Siouxsie and the Banshees had been recording their LP Juju. More recently playing to 5,000 people at the 2024 Visor fest in Murcia, Spain, with the Sun going down – Magical! Tony: Highlight for me was selling out Echoplex in LA at the end of our first US tour. Ian: I enjoy playing live so my personal highlights are: The first time we played The Marquee in Wardour Street – I felt it was a proper rock venue that I’d previously been to as a punter, it felt a bit surreal to me to be up on that stage in front of paying punters. Another surreal moment was my overseas debut at Club Isla near Valencia, which felt like an enormous gig to me. The Echoplex in LA was special. The festival in Murcia was too….so many great gigs. SLAG at the Echoplex in 2016. Photo by Terry Howick. Will: Playing live is definitely my favourite part of being in Sad Lovers & Giants. I love meeting the fans and other bands that we play with, I love seeing places around the world from a perspective that I wouldn’t be able to access without the network of promoters and friends that the band cultivates. I love feeling the connection with our audience during a performance – which feels like a celebration of the band, every time, and I feel privileged to be part of it and to help contribute to the legacy. In particular, I will always remember our US tour – which was a huge undertaking for the band – a chaotic yet rewarding experience of massive drives, downtown motels and passionate crowds. What’s next for the band? Garce: We play two gigs in Italy this October, then we put the final touches to the film for the rest of this year. The live album will be pressed and ready for release around then but the exact timing of everything depends on the film. Then we have a gig on a boat in Paris in March followed hopefully by a small tour of Portugal and Spain. After that there will inevitably be a series of gigs in all the usual places, namely Holland, Germany and Greece. Meanwhile the demo file will begin filling up again! § Sad Lovers & Giants’ new album The Weight of Forgotten Dreams is out now! Listen via Spotify and order here. Follow Sad Lovers & Giants Linktree Website Instagram Facebook Spotify Documentary Kickstarter Header photo by Simon Blanchard The post Down To The Wire — An Interview With Sad Lovers & Giants appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.album: Steven Bernstein: The Busiest Man in Show Biz
items.excerpt: A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦于Steven Bernstein三十年来在纽约音乐场景中的多重身份与跨界实践。他曾组建多个风格迥异的乐队，涵盖放克、灵魂乐、拉丁爵士及犹太教传统音乐，曾为Lou Reed、Lee "Scratch" Perry等横跨多种流派的艺术家编曲。值得一提的是他参与John Zorn的Radical Jewish Culture系列，将传统犹太祈祷歌曲与爵士、蓝调、摇滚相融合，并在Millennial Territory Orchestra中尝试幻灯小号这一罕见乐器。Sexmob乐队二十年来持续重新诠释从Leadbelly到Prince、从Nino Rota到James Brown的多元曲目，专辑Cultural Capital更是首张全原创作品。整体来看，Bernstein的创作展现出对音乐传统的开放态度与即兴探索精神，但文章以传记式梳理为主，缺乏对最新专辑具体音乐语言与演奏细节的深入评析。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.
items.label: Sunnyside SCS 1813
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / vocal improvisation / experimental piano
items._cn_summary: Ran Blake与Dominique Eade的合作专辑《Roots & Byways》延续了Blake标志性的解构式钢琴美学，将Max Roach、Mingus、Michel Legrand乃至Whitney Houston的流行金曲并置，以近乎医学影像式的听觉逻辑揭示不同素材之间隐秘的脉络关联。她不演奏传统意义上的诠释，而是剥离骨架让血肉与器官自行显现，使熟悉的作品焕发陌生的质感。Eade的声乐角色是这张专辑的关键变量：她既不像Jeanne Lee扎根于Billie Holiday的语汇，也不像Sara Serpa倾向于克制内敛，而是以逐音节雕琢的方式塑造旋律，并在明暗不同的曲目中持续渗透着鲜明的歌唱喜悦。这种喜悦成为专辑可亲近性的核心，让抽象的拼贴逻辑获得了情感落点。整体呈现出学院派爵士内部对曲目边界与演绎范式的持续实验。

items.body: American label Thesis have just released an overview of their recent output. Falling under the umbrella of their Subscription Series, this overview collects together four collaborations from four separate projects featuring some of the most well-known ambient and modern classical artists around: Tony Dekker, Great Lake Swimmers, Kinbrae, Angus MacRae, InsaDonjaKai, Anna Rose Carter, Dag Rosenqvist, Julianna Barwick and Rafael Anton Irisarri are all contributors. Bending synths bleed into Julianna Barwick’s saint-like vocals, drenched as they are in a swimming, translucent pool of reverb. Twinkling keys walk beside the lapping reverb, tentatively dipping their toes into its open waters and thus creating a slow whirl of echoing ripples. Although the atmosphere differs considerably as the listener moves from one track to the next, the general tone is light and carefree throughout, but that doesn’t make the music shallow. On the contrary, the tracks are infused with a deep level of introspection. Later tracks descend even deeper: on ‘Himmelgeist’, the piano’s mysterious air adds a cloak of intrigue as the air becomes colder and the strings stand as tall as pine trees in an October-lit forest. A piano wearing an icy dress will arrive later, its breath a ghost of a thin, white vapour, a winter cloud of dialogue puffing up and out of a cartoon character’s lips. Even as it shivers, the music is speaking, whispering quietly, with every note from the piano like a call in the dark, creating phrases which then become airborne words, sentences, conversations. So far in the subscription series the piano has been the dominant instrument, and that trend continues here. It doesn’t take on this mantle reluctantly…instead, it feels like it should be this way. Despite the gathering mystery, the music on this overview retains a warm, harmonious glow, its notes illuminated by orange tongues of flame and the dusky embers of a campfire. The music doesn’t have a dislocated, discordant bone in its body, and that leads the overview to contain nothing but low-key, remedial music. THESIS SUBSCRIPTION 02 (overview) by THESIS www.thesisproject.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: Thesis厂牌以订阅系列形式将四位艺术家的合作作品汇编成辑，参与者包括Julianna Barwick、Angus MacRae、Dag Rosenqvist、Rafael Anton Irisarri等。整体以钢琴为核心乐器，配合合成器绵延的混响层与弦乐，构筑出轻盈而内省的声景氛围。Barwick的人声在透明混响中漂浮，钢琴则以缓慢而审慎的步调展开叙事。评论用十月森林、冰封裙裾等意象勾勒曲目之间的氛围差异——从温暖营火般的和煦转向更幽深的沉思段落。音乐始终保持低饱和度的基调，没有尖锐的断裂或刺耳的对位，强调的是一种修复性、温和的聆听体验，适合作为日常的背景沉思之声。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online.
